explain: The scan touches every vector: 20.5M multiply-adds. The rerank touches only 200 vectors: 0.41M. So the shortlist scan is about 98% of the 20.9M total, and speeding it up (smaller D_s, ANN, binary) gives the biggest win.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
question: A model has 5as/h = 20 (short sequences, wide hidden size). Compared with GPT-3 (5as/h = 80), how much does selective recompute help it?
options: Exactly as much, it always saves 70%
More: it removes 80% because the model is wider
Nothing, selective recompute only works with sequence parallelism
Less: it removes 20/54 = 37% of activation memory
explain: Selective recompute removes the 5as/h part of 34 + 5as/h. For 5as/h = 20 that is 20/54 = 37%. The trick shines for long sequences and many heads, where the quadratic attention term dominates.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: FP8 training with Transformer Engine in Megatron Core
question: An H100 run needs FP8 together with optimizer CPU offload. Which recipe does Megatron Core accept?
options: tensorwise
blockwise
delayed
mxfp8
explain: The low-precision guide states that only delayed scaling is supported with optimizer CPU offload, and Megatron enforces it in its argument checks. mxfp8 also needs Blackwell.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Virtual addresses, page tables and the DTB, walked by hand
question: In the PAE split, why are the PD and PT indices 9 bits each?
options: Because Windows reserves 3 bits of every address
Each table is a 4 KB page holding 8-byte entries, so it has 512 entries, and 512 = 2^9
Because PAE pages are 9 KB
Because 9 bits is the size of a PID
explain: 4096 bytes per table divided by 8 bytes per entry gives 512 entries, and choosing one of 512 needs exactly 9 bits.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
question: Why does walking ActiveProcessLinks require subtracting 0xB8 from each Flink?
options: Because Windows encrypts pointers with 0xB8
Each Flink points to the links field inside the next EPROCESS, which sits 0xB8 bytes after the start of that structure
Because 0xB8 is the size of a page header
Because PIDs are stored 0xB8 bytes before each list
explain: Embedded list entries point at each other, not at the structures that contain them. To reach the structure's other fields you step back by the offset of the links field.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
question: Why might a registry value found in memory differ from the same value in the hive file on disk?
options: The disk version is always encrypted
Changes are held in memory and written to the hive file later, so memory can hold newer values
Registry hives are never loaded into memory
Memory stores only deleted keys
explain: The loaded hive in kernel memory is the live copy. The file on disk is updated when the system flushes, so recent changes may exist only in RAM.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it
question: Why must you deduplicate and filter timeliner output before reading it?
options: Several plugins report the same objects and some report several times per object, so raw rows overstate and repeat events
Because timeliner output is encrypted
Because duplicates mean the image is corrupt
Because body files cannot be sorted
explain: pslist and psscan both list every process, and in Volatility 3 2.28.2 timeliner also prints earlier rows again after each later plugin: PsList gave 476 rows for 34 processes in a full run, 34 when run alone. Group by object and keep the source plugin.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
question: A team patches their allocator from 4 to 8 classes per doubling. Which outcome should they expect?
options: Total memory always falls by about 9%
External fragmentation disappears because rounding is smaller
Allocation becomes slower because each request must search all classes
Worst-case internal waste falls from about 20% to about 11%, with more partly empty slabs to offset part of the gain
explain: Worst-case waste is just under 1/(n+1): 20% for n = 4, 11% for n = 8. But twice as many classes means twice as many places for partly filled slabs and cached objects to sit, so the net saving depends on the workload. Class lookup stays a computation, not a search.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
question: Ten threads each run `counter.fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` 1000 times; then main joins all ten and reads the counter. What does main see?
options: Exactly 10000
Any value from 1000 to 10000, since Relaxed does not order the increments
10000 on x86 but possibly less on ARM64
Undefined behavior, because Relaxed operations race
explain: Each fetch_add is atomic, so none are lost, and all of them sit in one modification order. Joining a thread creates happens-before from everything it did to the code after the join, so main reads the final value. Relaxed is not a race: races need a non-atomic access.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: A shutdown flag is set by one thread and polled by workers, which simply exit their loop when they see it. No other data is passed through the flag. Which ordering fits?
options: SeqCst, to make sure workers see it quickly
Release store and Acquire load
Relaxed
AcqRel on both store and load
explain: The flag carries no other data, so no happens-before edge is needed: Relaxed gives atomicity, and the model says nothing about speed anyway. If the workers had to read results or config written before the flag, you would upgrade to Release and Acquire. AcqRel is only for read-modify-write operations.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
question: CPU 1 calls synchronize_rcu() at time 10. Reader X started at time 8 and ends at 12; reader Y starts at 11 and ends at 30. Ignoring batching delays, when may synchronize_rcu() return?
options: At 30, after both readers
At 12, after X; Y need not be waited for
At 10, immediately, because readers take no locks
At 11, when Y starts
explain: Only pre-existing read-side critical sections count. X was running at time 10, so the grace period must cover it. Y started after the removal and cannot have obtained the removed pointer, so waiting for it would be wasted. Real implementations may return somewhat later because they batch requests.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Stack buffer overflow: when a copy runs past the end
question: Which change fixes `strcpy(buf, name)` for `char buf[8]` without silently corrupting memory for long names?
options: Make buf 64 bytes so normal names fit
Call strcpy twice to check the result
Use strncpy(buf, name, sizeof buf) and nothing else
Use snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, "%s", name), or reject names with strlen(name) >= sizeof buf
explain: A bigger buffer only raises the bar: a 65-byte name still overflows. strncpy stops at the size but leaves buf unterminated for long names, so the next read runs off the end. snprintf truncates and terminates; an explicit length check rejects the input.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
question: Code does `uint32_t n = w * h * 4; char *px = malloc(n);` for an image of width w and height h from a file, then writes w*h*4 bytes. What is the bug?
options: None: malloc checks the size
The bug is only that malloc's result is not checked
malloc can't allocate images
w * h * 4 can wrap in 32 bits, so px is smaller than the bytes later written
explain: For a large enough w and h the product exceeds 4,294,967,295 and wraps, so the allocation is small. The later writes use the true size and overflow. Checking malloc's result for NULL does not help because malloc succeeds. Fix: check each multiplication (calloc or __builtin_mul_overflow) and limit w and h.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Finding memory bugs: warnings, sanitizers, Valgrind and fuzzing
question: Why is AddressSanitizer usually not enabled in production builds?
options: It only works on Windows
Its documentation says the runtime is a testing tool not designed for security-sensitive production use, and it costs about 2x speed and more memory
It produces many false alarms
It removes bounds checks
explain: ASan is precise (its docs say no false alarms) but slows programs about 2x, uses extra memory, and its runtime was not built with production security constraints in mind. It belongs in testing, CI (continuous integration: the build and tests that run on every change) and fuzzing.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
question: You switch from batch hard to batch all without changing anything else and validation mAP drops. Which change would most directly test the 'washed out' explanation?
options: Increase the margin to 1.0
Average the loss only over triplets with non-zero loss
Square the distances
Use K = 1
explain: If zero-loss triplets dilute the gradient, averaging only the active terms removes the dilution. Hermans and colleagues ran this test and the non-zero average performed much better than the plain average.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
question: A new hash map is 2x faster than the old one in a benchmark with 1000 keys, but the service using 50 million keys sees no gain. What is the most plausible reason?
options: At 1000 keys both maps fit in cache, so the benchmark measured hashing and probing on hot data; at 50 million keys both are dominated by cache misses to DRAM
The benchmark forgot DoNotOptimize
The service has more threads
Hash maps are O(1), so size cannot matter
explain: A small key set keeps the whole table in L1 or L2, where instruction counts dominate. A huge table makes nearly every probe a DRAM miss, and a design that saves instructions but makes as many misses gains little. Big-O hides exactly this constant. Sweep the size before trusting the 2x.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
question: An agentic batch has 8 trajectories per group; one takes 40 turns while the rest finish in 3. Which setting keeps engine slots busiest while that trajectory runs?
options: --rollout-submission-granularity group, so the group stays together
--pause-generation-mode abort, to kill stragglers
--update-weights-interval 0
--rollout-submission-granularity sample, so each finished trajectory frees its own slot
explain: With sample granularity, the seven short trajectories free their slots as soon as they finish, and new groups start in them. With group granularity, all eight slots stay reserved until the 40-turn trajectory returns. Abort mode is rejected under fully async.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned policies leave a gap: LRU versus Belady's MIN
question: A 3-slot cache holds X, Y and Z. Their next requests are: X in 7 requests, Y never, Z in 2 requests. A miss for W arrives. What does Belady's MIN evict?
options: Z, because it was used least recently
X, because it is needed later than Z
Y, because it is never requested again
W is not admitted, because MIN only evicts on hits
explain: MIN evicts the object whose next request is furthest away, and never counts as furthest of all. Recency (option one) is LRU's rule, not MIN's. X is a reasonable second choice but loses to Y.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
question: Using Lykouris and Vassilvitskii's result, what happens to their predictor-augmented Marker algorithm if the oracle's predictions become arbitrarily bad?
options: It stays within O(log k) of optimal, the same bound as classic Marker without predictions
Its competitive ratio grows without bound
It becomes exactly as good as Belady's MIN
It refuses to evict
explain: The point of the construction is robustness: the ratio improves as prediction error falls, but it is always capped by O(log k), which is achievable with no oracle at all. Blindly following the oracle has no such cap.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: a test device, a proxy and the app's own files
question: In the Starbucks case, the app kept its OAuth token in the Keychain, yet the password still leaked. Which MASVS control did the app fail?
options: MASVS-STORAGE-2: the app prevents leakage of sensitive data, here through a log file
MASVS-NETWORK-1, because the password was sent in cleartext
MASVS-RESILIENCE-1, because the phone could be jailbroken
MASVS-CRYPTO-1, because the Keychain is weak
explain: Storing the token securely satisfies part of STORAGE-1, but the password reached a log through the crash reporter: a leak, which is STORAGE-2. There was no network flaw in the advisory, and resilience controls would not stop an app from writing its own log.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code
question: An app's WebView exposes `addJavascriptInterface(Bridge(), 'native')` and loads only `https://help.example.com`. The help site embeds a third-party chat widget in an iframe. What can the widget's script do?
options: Call the bridge's @JavascriptInterface methods, because the object is injected into every frame, including iframes
Nothing: iframes cannot see objects added by the app
Only read the page's text
Call the bridge only if the user taps inside the iframe
explain: Android's guidance says addJavascriptInterface injects the object into every frame, including iframes, with no way to check the calling frame's origin. Third-party content on your own page therefore reaches your native code. addWebMessageListener with origin rules, or no bridge, fixes it.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Running a mobile app assessment end to end, and where to practise
question: The scope says 'profile MAS-L2+P'. During testing you find the app has no jailbreak detection and no obfuscation. How should these appear in the report?
options: As informational observations at most, since MAS-R is not in the agreed profile and their absence is not in itself a vulnerability
As high-severity findings under MASVS-STORAGE
They should not be mentioned at all
As critical, because the backend can be called directly
explain: Resilience controls belong to MAS-R. Under L2+P they are optional defence in depth, so at most an observation, perhaps with a note on when they would matter (fraud, cheating). Calling the API directly is a backend question, answered by server-side checks, not by client obfuscation.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Decoupled RoPE: why position breaks absorption
question: A colleague's absorbed MLA decoder applies RoPE at position t to the full 512-wide absorbed query, then dots it with the cached latents. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, RoPE commutes with the latent projection
It only fails for contexts longer than 4K
The rotation now acts in latent space, which does not equal rotating each head's keys; position information is wrong and the scores no longer match the trained model
The cache size doubles
explain: RoPE in MLA must only touch the decoupled 64-wide parts. The content part was trained without rotation, and a rotation applied in the 512-wide latent space is not the per-head offset rotation $R_{j-t}$ of the key, so the scores no longer match the trained model. Lesson 5 runs this exact bug.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
question: A GQA layer like those in Meta's Llama models has 32 query heads, 8 KV heads and $d_h = 128$. What latent size rewrites it exactly as MLA, and what happens to its cache?
options: 128, and the cache shrinks 16x
4,096, and the cache doubles
1,024, and the cache halves
2,048, and the cache stays the same size
explain: The latent is the stacked keys and values, $2 g d_h = 2 \times 8 \times 128 = 2048$, which is exactly what GQA already caches per token per layer. Saving memory needs a further compression step.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
question: Using the simplified bandwidth model, which change most reduces the extra bytes read per step when 32 distinct adapters share each batch?
options: Raising the batch size to 64
Sorting rows by adapter
Using more prefill tokens per batch
Halving every adapter's rank
explain: Extra traffic is proportional to (distinct adapters) x rank. Halving the rank halves it. Sorting is required for SGMV to work but does not change how many adapter bytes must be read, and a bigger batch with more tenants can add distinct adapters.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: A LangChain `MultiQueryRetriever` with defaults is called through `invoke` over a base retriever with k = 5. What comes back?
options: The 5 highest RRF-scored documents
Up to 15 unique documents from the 3 rewrites, in the order they were retrieved
Exactly 20 documents including duplicates
Only the documents that appear in all 3 lists
explain: With include_original=False, 3 rewrites are searched (sequentially on the sync path) and the unique union is returned, up to 3 x 5 = 15 documents, in query order. There is no rank fusion and no truncation to k.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
question: Why does the pipeline run duoBERT on monoBERT's top 50 instead of directly on BM25's top 1000?
options: duoBERT cannot read passages that BM25 retrieved
Pairwise scoring grows as k(k-1): 1000 candidates would need 999,000 inferences instead of 2450
duoBERT is less accurate than monoBERT, so it should see fewer documents
BM25 scores must be normalized before a pairwise model can use them
explain: Pairwise cost is quadratic in the list length. On 1000 candidates, duoBERT would need 1000 x 999 = 999,000 inferences per query, about 290 times the 3450 that monoBERT plus duoBERT on 50 use. Putting the quadratic model last, on a short list, is exactly the cascade idea.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: Why does Margin-MSE train the student on score margins instead of making it reproduce the teacher's raw scores?
options: Different architectures naturally produce scores on different scales; only the ordering matters, and the margin preserves it
Raw scores are not available from cross-encoders
Margins are cheaper to compute at query time
MSE cannot be applied to raw scores
explain: A dot-product bi-encoder or ColBERT produces scores on a very different scale from a cross-encoder. Forcing the same raw values fights the architecture. Ranking only needs the student to separate relevant from non-relevant by the same amount, which is what the margin captures.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: At depth k = 2 in DeepSeek-V3's scheme, which inputs does the module use for position i, and which token does it predict?
options: h_i from the main model and Emb(t_i+1); predicts t_i+2
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+3); predicts t_i+3
Only Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
explain: Depth k combines h at depth k - 1 with the embedding of t(i+k) and predicts t(i+k+1). For k = 2 that is h from depth 1, Emb(t(i+2)), and target t(i+3).

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: You serve a Gloeckle-style 4-token model with greedy decoding and enable self-speculative decoding with all 4 heads. What happens to the generated text?
options: It becomes more diverse because heads 2 to 4 inject their own choices
It is identical to greedy decoding with head 1; only the number of forward passes drops
It is identical only if every draft is accepted
It degrades slightly, which is the price of a 3x speedup
explain: Every emitted token is one that head 1 would have chosen given the same prefix: drafts are kept only when they match head 1's prediction, and the first mismatch is replaced by head 1's token. Acceptance rate changes speed, never content.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
question: A colleague raises Muon's Newton-Schulz steps from 5 to 10 to get a more exactly orthogonal update. Based on the Moonlight report, what should they expect?
options: Noticeably lower loss, since the update is now exactly U V-transpose
Divergence, because the tuned polynomial is unstable after 5 steps
A more accurate orthogonalization but no better model, at twice the Newton-Schulz cost
No change at all in the update, because the iteration converged after 5 steps
explain: Moonlight reports that $N = 10$ gives a more accurate orthogonalization than $N = 5$ but does not improve performance, so they kept 5. With the tuned coefficients the values keep bouncing within roughly $[0.7, 1.2]$, so the update does change, just not in a way that helps.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon in a real training stack: parameter groups, sharding and code
question: A model uses one fused $3d \times d$ QKV weight, and the team gives it to Muon. What changes if they split it into three $d \times d$ matrices?
options: Nothing: orthogonalizing the stack is the same as orthogonalizing each block
Muon fails on the fused weight because it is not square
Splitting only matters for memory: the update is identical but stored differently
Each projection gets its own orthogonalized update, so a strong direction in, say, the query gradient no longer dictates the singular directions shared by all three
explain: Orthogonalizing a stacked matrix equalizes singular values of the *stack*, so the three blocks share one set of right singular vectors and one budget. Separately, each gets $U_q V_q^\top$, $U_k V_k^\top$, $U_v V_v^\top$. The Muon post reports the split version trains transformers better. Rectangular matrices are fine for Muon.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: The muP rules, layer by layer
question: Which of these is a vector-like parameter in a Transformer whose width is d_model?
options: A LayerNorm gain vector of length d_model
The query projection W_q (d_model x d_model)
The MLP up-projection (d_model x 4 d_model)
A scalar temperature applied to the logits
explain: A LayerNorm gain has exactly one dimension that grows with width, so it is vector-like and keeps a constant Adam LR. W_q and the MLP matrices have two infinite dimensions (matrix-like). A scalar has none, so it is scalar-like and held constant.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
question: Your training loop sets the learning rate with `for pg in opt.param_groups: pg['lr'] = base_lr * warmup(step)`, using a MuAdamW optimizer. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; MuAdamW recomputes width scaling every step
Only the embedding learning rate changes
Every group, including the hidden-weight groups, gets the same learning rate, so the 1/m width scaling is lost and the model behaves like SP
Training becomes deterministic
explain: MuAdamW encodes muP by splitting parameters into groups whose `lr` was already divided by the width multiplier. Assigning an absolute value overwrites that. The README's rule is to set lr relative to the group's current value (`pg['lr'] *= 2`); for warmup, store each group's initial lr and multiply it by the warmup factor.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin
question: In the cost model, sleeping costs C = 5 units and you spin for a budget B = 5 before sleeping. The lock turns out to be held for W = 3 units. What do you pay?
options: 5 units, because you always sleep eventually
10 units
8 units
3 units: the lock frees up during the spin
explain: W = 3 is within the budget, so you spin 3 units, take the lock, and never sleep. That equals the best in hindsight, min(3, 5) = 3.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
question: A table has 1 row that has been updated 3 times since it was inserted, and no VACUUM has run. How many tuples for that row are on disk?
explain: The insert created one tuple and each of the 3 updates wrote another, so there are 4 tuples. Only the newest has xmax = 0; the other 3 wait for VACUUM.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Paying for versions: VACUUM, HOT updates and XID wraparound
question: An UPDATE changes only a non-indexed `last_seen` column, and the page has free space. What does HOT save compared with a normal update?
options: It avoids writing a new tuple version at all
It avoids new index entries, and lets old versions be pruned without VACUUM
It skips writing to the WAL
It makes the update visible to concurrent snapshots
explain: HOT still writes a new tuple version (MVCC requires it), but on the same page and without new index entries. Intermediate versions can be pruned during normal page access.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Scoring whole sequences: transitions and Viterbi by hand
question: Your BIO tagger has no CRF and sometimes emits `O I-ORG I-ORG`. Which response still leaves that sequence possible?
options: Add a CRF layer so the training loss sees label transitions and Viterbi cannot take an invalid one
Switch to BIOES so the output layer has 17 labels instead of 9
Keep the independent softmax but mask out transitions the scheme forbids during decoding
Decode with a beam that only extends well-formed BIO prefixes
explain: BIOES makes the tag set larger and the end of a span explicit, but with independent per-token softmaxes nothing rules out an impossible sequence: you can still emit O then I-ORG, now with 17 labels. The other three all make the invalid path unreachable, either in the loss or in the decoder.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Three branches: compress, select, and slide
question: With NSA's settings ($d=16$, $n=16$, $l'=64$, $w=512$), which term of the per-query key count dominates at a 1M-token context?
options: The compressed tokens, about $t/d \approx 65{,}500$
The selected tokens, $nl' = 1024$
The window, $w = 512$
All three are equal
explain: Selection and window are fixed sizes. Compression grows linearly with $t$ at rate $1/d$, so at long context it dominates: about 65,534 of roughly 67,070 keys at 1,048,576 tokens.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
question: Why does `cmp_mask` compare the query position with the last token of each compression block, not the first?
options: Because the last token always has the largest key
To make the compressed keys differentiable
It is arbitrary; either choice gives a valid causal model
Because a summary mixes all l tokens of its block, so using it before the block ends would leak future tokens into the past
explain: The MLP reads the whole block, so its output depends on every token in it. A query that saw the summary before the block ended would get information from tokens after itself, which breaks causal training and cannot be reproduced at decode time.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
question: Your service computes pHash with library X; a partner sends pHashes computed with library Y for the same images. Distances between matching pairs are around 30 of 64. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The partner's images were heavily edited
Hamming distance is undefined across libraries
pHash is random by design
Libraries differ in details such as resize filter, mean versus median and whether DC is included, so their bits are not comparable
explain: pHash is a family of variants. Krawetz uses a mean without DC, ImageHash a median with DC, and resampling filters differ too. Meta's PDQ documentation (PDQ is Meta's open-source 256-bit perceptual hash, the subject of lesson 5) makes the same point: even one algorithm in different languages can give different hashes, so it defines conformance against the reference implementation.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: The three contracts: policy, generation and environment interfaces
question: You write a custom environment that runs unit tests. It returns `rewards` as a dict `{"tests": ..., "style": ...}`. GDPO training fails to find the components. What is the most likely bug?
options: Environments may only return a single Tensor
The keys must use the reward/ prefix, for example reward/tests
Rewards must be Python lists, not tensors
Multi-reward environments must set terminateds to all zeros
explain: The environments guide states that each key of a multi-reward dict must use the reward/ prefix. The rollout then stores the summed total_reward and each named component for GDPO.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Where the attacker stands: on-path, off-path and on your LAN
question: A host 3,000 km away sends a packet with a forged source address to your server. Which statement is true?
options: It is on-path, because its packet reached your server
It will receive your server's reply, because the source address is in the packet
It cannot reach your server at all without being on the same LAN
It cannot see the reply, so any secret your server puts in the reply (such as a sequence number) must be guessed
explain: Replies go to the forged address, not to the sender. That is the defining limit of an off-path attacker, and why protocols put unguessable values (TCP sequence numbers, DNS transaction IDs) in places only the real peer can see.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DNS cache poisoning: the race and the birthday maths
question: Why does a forged reply need to arrive before the real one?
options: Because the first reply that passes the checks completes the query, and the real answer arriving later is dropped
Because the resolver checks timestamps
Because UDP delivers only one packet per port
Because the real server would detect the forgery
explain: Once a matching reply is accepted the query is no longer pending, so the later genuine reply has nothing to match and is discarded. The attacker is racing the real server, and only the attacker knows a race is happening.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: RPKI and route origin validation
question: Why does RFC 6811 call origin validation mainly protection against misconfiguration?
options: Because a deliberate attacker can forge a path ending in the authorised origin AS, which ROV accepts
Because ROAs are unsigned
Because ROV only works for IPv6
Because routers ignore Invalid routes by default
explain: ROV checks the last AS in the path and nothing else. A careful attacker appends the legitimate origin to their announcement. Accidental hijacks, such as the 2008 YouTube event, carry the wrong origin and are caught.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Scanning, as defenders see it
question: In conn.log you see thousands of records from one internal workstation, each to a different internal IP on port 445, nearly all with history S and state S0. What is the most reasonable reading?
options: Normal file sharing
The workstation's antivirus updating
A horizontal scan from a possibly compromised internal host; most targets did not answer
A SYN flood against the workstation
explain: One source, one port, many destinations, almost no answers: a horizontal scan, the pattern of worms and of attackers moving laterally. That it comes from inside makes it urgent; isolate and examine the workstation.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Intrusion detection, network monitoring, and where to practise
question: A Suricata sensor is connected to a switch's mirror port. A rule with action 'drop' matches an attack. What happens?
options: Nothing is blocked: a passive sensor sees copies of traffic, so it can alert but not stop the original packets
The rule fails to load
The attack packets are dropped
The switch shuts the port
explain: A sensor on a mirror (spanning) port is passive by definition: it receives copies. Blocking requires an inline deployment where traffic must pass through the sensor, as NIST SP 800-94 describes.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Wireshark display filters: asking precise questions of packets
question: A filter `http.user_agent matches "python"` shows packets whose User-Agent is 'Python-urllib/3.12'. A colleague expected it not to match because of the capital P. Who is right and why?
options: The colleague: matches is case-sensitive like grep
You: matches is case-insensitive by default in Wireshark; add (?-i) to make it case-sensitive
Neither: matches only works on numbers
The colleague: User-Agent values are always lower-cased by the dissector
explain: The manual says matches applies a PCRE2 (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions) pattern that is case-insensitive by default, and shows (?-i) to force case sensitivity. contains, by contrast, compares exact bytes.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Suricata in depth: how rules match, EVE output and tuning
question: An alert fired on an HTTP response. In eve.json, how do you find that same connection's HTTP request, file information and byte counts?
options: Search for the same signature ID
Select every record with the alert's flow_id
Search for the same timestamp
Read fast.log, which contains the full request
explain: Suricata gives all records about one flow the same flow_id; its EVE documentation shows jq selecting on flow_id to gather the alert, http, fileinfo, anomaly and flow events together. A signature ID matches every flow that triggered the rule, and timestamps differ between event types.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Finding beacons with robust statistics: the RITA approach
question: Your beacon report's top entry: 2,800 internal hosts each contact the same destination every 3,600 seconds exactly, with identical response sizes. What is the best conclusion?
options: A company-wide compromise: isolate all 2,800 hosts
Almost certainly managed software checking for updates or reporting telemetry; verify the destination and owner, then allowlist it so real outliers surface
A DNS tunnel
Capture loss on the sensor
explain: Very high prevalence plus perfect regularity is the signature of software deployed everywhere, such as an updater. Confirm what it is (destination owner, process on one host) and allowlist it. A real implant usually shows the opposite pattern: regular timing to a destination that only one or a few hosts ever contact.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: From bits on a wire to packets
question: A packet's header says it comes from address A. What does that prove about who sent it?
options: It proves the packet came from A, because routers check the sender
It proves the packet came from A's network, but not which device
Nothing by itself: the sender's own software wrote that field
It proves the packet came from A only if the payload is longer than the header
explain: The header is just bytes written by whoever built the packet. Some networks filter packets with impossible source addresses (you will meet this as ingress filtering), but the basic protocols do not verify the sender. Treat a source address as a claim, not a proof.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Routing: gateways, TTL, traceroute and BGP
question: A router has routes for `208.65.152.0/22` (to A), `208.65.153.0/24` (to B) and `0.0.0.0/0` (to C). Where does it send a packet for `208.65.155.4`?
options: B, because /24 is the longest prefix in the table
C, because only exact matches count
A, because 208.65.155.4 is inside the /22 (152.0 to 155.255) but not inside the /24
It drops the packet as ambiguous
explain: Longest prefix match only chooses among prefixes that actually contain the address. 208.65.152.0/22 spans 208.65.152.0 to 208.65.155.255, so it matches; the /24 covers only 208.65.153.x. The default route also matches but is shorter.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTP: requests, responses, headers and cookies
question: A log shows 3,000 requests in two minutes from one IP, almost all `404 Not Found`, for paths like `/admin`, `/backup.zip`, `/.git/config`. What is most likely happening?
options: A user with a broken bookmark
Automated scanning for forgotten or sensitive files
A denial-of-service attack using amplification
Normal search engine indexing
explain: Thousands of guessed paths in a short time, mostly missing, are the fingerprint of a content discovery scanner looking for admin panels, backups and exposed repositories. The rare 200 among them is the line to investigate first.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A 4-node server's distance table shows 10 on the diagonal and 20 everywhere else. What is the safest reading?
options: Every remote access costs exactly twice a local one
Remote access is roughly twice as costly as local, but firmware tables can be inaccurate, so measure
The machine is actually UMA because all remote entries are equal
explain: SLIT values are relative estimates normalized to 10 for local access. Drepper shows a real table that reported 20 for every pair even though some pairs had to be two hops apart. Use the table as a hint and benchmark when placement matters.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: A database pins each worker to one node and places every buffer with explicit mbind policies. Profiling shows time spent in page faults on pages that never move. What is the most likely fix?
options: Enable MPOL_INTERLEAVE on all buffers
Use smaller pages so faults are cheaper
Disable automatic NUMA balancing for this workload
explain: These are NUMA hinting faults from automatic balancing sampling pages that are already correctly placed. The kernel docs recommend disabling balancing when the workload is already bound to NUMA nodes.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
question: A service writes 300 TB per year to a 1 TB drive rated for 10,000 P/E cycles. The drive's FDP statistics show media bytes written are 5x host bytes. Roughly how long until rated wear-out?
options: About 6.7 years
About 33 years
About 1.3 years
Never, wear leveling prevents it
explain: Lifetime host writes = 1 TB x 10,000 / 5 = 2,000 TB. At 300 TB per year that is 2000/300, about 6.7 years. Halving A to 2.5 would double it.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
question: Why does DETR not need NMS at test time?
options: Its object queries are fixed to non-overlapping image regions
It applies NMS inside the transformer decoder
One-to-one Hungarian matching during training gives each object only one positive prediction, so other slots learn to predict 'no object'
It only predicts one object per image
explain: Object queries are learned embeddings, not fixed regions. Because the matching assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one slot, a second slot covering the same object is trained toward the no-object class. The DETR paper reports that adding NMS helps early decoder layers but slightly hurts AP at the last layer.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Batching writes: the cost versus latency dial
question: To cut latency further, an engineer changes the Agent to acknowledge a Produce request as soon as it lands in the in-memory buffer. What does this break?
options: Ordering within a partition
Nothing, since S3 is durable
Compaction, because files get smaller
Durability: if the Agent crashes before the PUT, acknowledged records are lost
explain: The buffer is memory in a stateless process. WarpStream never acknowledges a write until it is in object storage and committed to the metadata store, which is what lets it lose every Agent without losing acknowledged data. Acking from memory turns a crash into data loss.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
question: Checkout p99 reads 1.3 s and the orders database p99 reads 0.9 s, both rising in the same minute. What do the metrics alone establish?
options: That checkout requests are waiting on the database
That the database is the root cause, since it is the deepest component
That the two are correlated in time, but not that any single checkout request waited on the database
Nothing, because percentiles from different services are never comparable
explain: Metrics are per-component aggregates with no request identity, so simultaneity is a hypothesis, not a causal link. The slow checkout requests and the slow queries may even be disjoint sets. A trace carries parent and child spans and settles it for one request.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
question: Why does DBNet replace the hard threshold with a sigmoid of k(P - T)?
options: It makes inference faster than a comparison
It lets gradients flow so the network can learn a per-pixel threshold map
It removes the need for the probability map
It guarantees that adjacent words never merge
explain: A step function has zero gradient almost everywhere, so a threshold inside it cannot be learned. The steep sigmoid approximates the step but stays differentiable. At inference the paper actually drops this path and uses a constant threshold on P.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The kernel/user boundary: rings and the system call door
question: Which bug is usually the most severe for a multi-user Linux server?
options: A crash in a user's text editor
A memory bug in a kernel system call that any process can make
A memory bug in a setuid program that only root can run
A typo in a log message
explain: A kernel bug reachable from any process can bypass every permission check, for every user and every container on the host. A setuid program that only root can run gives an attacker nothing new.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: AppArmor: path-based profiles that confine one program
question: What is the key design difference between AppArmor and SELinux?
options: AppArmor confines users, SELinux confines programs
AppArmor only works on Windows
AppArmor rules name paths a program uses; SELinux rules name types stored in labels on subjects and objects
SELinux is discretionary and AppArmor is mandatory
explain: Both are mandatory and both confine programs. AppArmor writes rules in terms of paths, which makes profiles readable; SELinux writes them in terms of types, so a file's label travels with it.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Namespaces and cgroups: the building blocks of containers
question: A process is root inside a user namespace (mapped to UID 1000 outside). It tries to set the system's calendar clock. What happens?
options: It changes the clock only for the container
It succeeds, because it has all capabilities in its namespace
It succeeds only inside a time namespace
It fails, because capabilities in a user namespace apply only to resources governed by that namespace, and the system clock is not one
explain: user_namespaces(7) uses this very example: changing the system time is governed by CAP_SYS_TIME in the initial namespace. Time namespaces offset only the boot and monotonic clocks.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Secure boot, module signing and kernel hardening knobs
question: An attacker has root on a server with kernel lockdown enabled and module signature enforcement on. What stops them loading a rootkit module they compiled?
options: Secure boot scans the disk at runtime
The rootkit must be in /lib/modules
The kernel refuses modules that are not validly signed with a trusted key, even for root
Nothing: root can do anything
explain: With enforcement, the kernel itself checks the signature at load time. Root controls the filesystem but does not hold the signing key, so the module is refused.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: What OSINT is, and what it is for
question: Under the Berkeley Protocol, which of these is closed-source information?
options: A company's published annual report
A satellite image anyone can buy from a commercial provider
Details an investigator learns by messaging an employee on a social network
A public video on a video-sharing site
explain: The Protocol treats information acquired "through communication with" internet users as closed source. Buying satellite imagery is fine: open source includes what the public can purchase.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
question: A `site:northwind.example filetype:pdf` search returns nothing. What can you conclude?
options: Northwind has no PDF files on any server
Google has not shown any indexed PDFs for that query; others may exist or be unindexed
Northwind blocks Google entirely
The query syntax was wrong
explain: Google documents that site: results are not always exhaustive. An empty result is evidence about the index, not about the server.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Verifying images and claims: provenance, reposts and hashes
question: Why can a SHA-256 hash not find a resized repost of a photo, while dHash can?
options: SHA-256 is too slow for images
dHash uses a secret key
SHA-256 changes completely when any byte changes; dHash compares brightness patterns that resizing keeps
SHA-256 only works on text
explain: Cryptographic hashes are designed so any change gives an unrelated hash. dHash records which neighbour is brighter, a pattern that survives resizing and uniform brightness changes.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Archiving: capturing evidence that will still be trusted later
question: What does a matching SHA-256 hash, recomputed months later, prove?
options: That the web page was truthful
That the page never changed online
That the stored file is unchanged since its hash was recorded
Who wrote the page
explain: A hash proves integrity of the stored copy from the moment it was hashed. Truth, authorship and the live page's history need other evidence.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
question: A colleague says: "Ninja must re-scan all #include lines before every build, so a no-op build (one where nothing changed) of 10,000 files is slow." What does Ninja actually do?
options: It runs the preprocessor on every file to find includes
It ignores headers and only tracks .cpp timestamps
It reuses header lists the compiler reported in earlier builds (depfiles), stored in its own database
It asks CMake to recompute header dependencies on every run
explain: With deps = gcc, Ninja reads each depfile right after the compile and saves a compact form in an internal database, so a no-op build only has to stat files (ask the operating system for each file's modification time, without reading it), not preprocess them.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
question: Your branch passes all tests locally. CI on your PR fails in a test file you never touched. Since you branched, `main` gained 20 commits. What is the most likely explanation to check first?
options: The CI runner is broken and you should ask a maintainer to rerun it
CI tests the merge of your branch into the current `main`, and your change interacts badly with something that landed since you branched
GitHub Actions only runs tests in files changed by the PR, so it must be a caching bug
Your local Python is newer, so CI should be ignored
explain: For `pull_request` events GitHub tests the merge commit `refs/pull/N/merge`. Rebase or merge the latest `main` locally and rerun the tests to reproduce. Blaming the runner first is how real failures get dismissed; and Actions runs whatever the workflow says, not only changed files.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
question: A test passes alone, passes in file order, but fails about one run in five under `pytest -n 4` (pytest-xdist). Locally with `-p randomly` it also fails for some seeds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The test is too slow and xdist times it out
It depends on state another test sets up or leaves behind, so it breaks when the order or the worker process changes
xdist uses threads, which makes Python tests nondeterministic
Exit code 5 from xdist workers
explain: Failing under reordering and under parallel workers is the signature of order or state dependence. The pytest docs note that xdist spawns processes, not threads, and that tests relying on data from a previous test break when that test is on a different worker.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
question: A repository has no branch protection or rulesets. A maintainer submits Request changes on your PR. Can someone with merge rights still merge it?
options: No, Request changes always blocks merging until the reviewer approves
Yes, without a rule requiring reviews, Request changes is informational
No, GitHub requires at least two approvals by default
Only after the reviewer dismisses their own review
explain: GitHub's docs say Request changes is purely informational unless a ruleset or classic branch protection rule requires pull request reviews. The social signal still matters: merging over an unresolved request is a team decision, not a tool one.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
question: Under Contributor Covenant 2.1, a contributor gets a Warning with a 30-day no-contact period. A week later they message the person who reported them on social media to explain themselves. What follows?
options: Nothing: social media is outside the project's spaces
It is allowed because the contributor is apologising
It breaks the Warning's terms, which cover external channels like social media, and can lead to a temporary or permanent ban
The Warning is cancelled and replaced by a Correction
explain: A Warning forbids interaction with the people involved for a set period, including unsolicited contact and external channels like social media. The text says violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
question: Your branch has commits P (parser), T (tests), then a `fixup! parser` commit F. After `git rebase -i --autosquash upstream/main`, what does the todo list contain?
options: pick P, pick T, fixup F
pick P, pick T, squash F
fixup F, pick P, pick T
pick P, fixup F, pick T
explain: Autosquash moves each `fixup!` commit directly after the commit whose title it names and turns its `pick` into `fixup`. So F lands between P and T. `squash` is used only for `squash!` commits, and a fixup never runs before its target.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
question: A bank modifies a GPL-3.0 command-line tool and runs it on internal servers only. An employee asks for the modified source to publish on GitHub. What does the license require?
options: The bank must publish the source within a reasonable time
Nothing: in-house use is not conveying, so no source obligation arises
The bank must give the source to that employee only
The bank must switch to the AGPL
explain: Using a program inside one organization is not conveying, and the GPL FAQ confirms an organization can use a modified version internally without releasing it. Obligations start only when copies go to others.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
question: Which PR description gives a reviewer the most to act on?
options: "About 20% faster on my machine."
"Encode is 17.2% faster (median of 10 interleaved runs each, p=0.000 via benchstat, idle linux/amd64); cache adds one entry per type."
"Encode is much faster now; see the flame graph screenshot."
"Benchmarks pass in CI, so performance is fine."
explain: Only the second states the method (10 interleaved runs, median), a significance result, the setup, and the cost. The others give no way to judge noise or to rerun the experiment, and "CI passes" usually checks correctness, not speed.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
question: You run `git grep -n parse_config` in a project and get no hits, but you can see `parse_config` in a file in your editor. Which explanation is most likely?
options: The file is untracked or ignored, and git grep searches tracked files only
git grep is case-insensitive by default
git grep needs `-r` to search subdirectories
git grep only searches the last commit, not the working tree
explain: By default git grep searches tracked files in the working tree. A new file you have not added, or one matched by .gitignore, is invisible to it. Use `--untracked` (and `--no-exclude-standard` for ignored files). Recursion is already the default, and the working tree, not HEAD, is searched.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
question: Which of these is the strongest version of the *Reproducible* property?
options: You copied the failing lines out of your app into the report
You described the steps carefully from memory
You ran the exact snippet in the report in a fresh environment and saw the same error
explain: Reproducible means tested. Copying lines out of a larger program often drops something they depended on, and memory is unreliable. Stack Overflow's guide suggests transporting the example to a fresh environment to confirm it still fails, because you may have accidentally fixed or changed the bug while trimming.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
question: A contributor's PR adds a new public function `parse_duration()` but no caller, promising "the caller comes in the next PR". What is the strongest review concern?
options: The PR is too large and should be split further
The PR is too small to judge: without a use, reviewers cannot tell if the API is right
New functions always need a separate design document first
It should be a draft because it has no tests
explain: Google's guide on small CLs (changelists, Google's internal name for a change sent for review, like a PR) says a change should not be so small that its implications are hard to understand; adding an API with a usage lets reviewers see how it will be used and avoids checking in unused APIs.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
question: Which change would most increase batch size for a contiguous-allocation server?
options: Use a faster attention kernel
Increase the maximum sequence length so fewer requests are rejected
Allocate KV memory in small fixed-size pieces on demand instead of one max-length chunk per request
Sort waiting requests by prompt length before batching them
explain: Waste comes from reserving for the worst case in one contiguous piece. Allocating small fixed-size pieces only when tokens arrive removes reservation and external fragmentation and caps internal fragmentation at one piece per sequence. That is exactly PagedAttention's design.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: What a penetration test is, and what it is not
question: Why does NIST say a pentest can find risk that a vulnerability scan misses?
options: Pentests use secret tools that scanners lack
Testers confirm findings and combine several weaknesses into one path to greater access
Pentests always scan more ports
Scanners only work on Windows
explain: SP 800-115 stresses combinations: two medium issues (a default password and a reachable database) can together be critical. Scanners report each item alone and only as a possibility.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: what your DNS tells the world
question: Why is passive DNS recon nearly invisible to the target?
options: DNS is encrypted
DNS servers do not log queries
dig hides the source address
The tester's queries go to their own resolver, and the target's authoritative servers only see that resolver asking, like any other visitor
explain: Recursive resolution means the authoritative server sees the resolver's address. Many queries for a domain are normal background, so there is little to detect.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: From scan XML to a findings table
question: A row reads `10.0.0.9 | 3389 | ms-wbt-server | | 3 | -`. What should you conclude?
options: Remote Desktop is definitely running
The host is vulnerable
Port 3389 is open, but the service name is a port-number lookup with low confidence; confirm what is actually listening before reporting it
The scan failed
explain: Empty product, conf 3 and no CPE mean version detection did not identify the service. The port is open; the label is only the usual service for 3389.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Kali Linux and what its tool categories are for
question: A SOC analyst sees a burst of requests whose user agent names a well-known web vulnerability scanner. What is the sensible first question?
options: Is an authorised scan or pentest running from that address in this window?
Which Kali version are they using?
Should we block all Linux users?
Can we scan them back?
explain: Check the test schedule and authorised source addresses first. If no test explains it, treat it as hostile reconnaissance; user agents are easy to fake in either direction.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
question: Why does stackcollapse-perf.pl strip offsets like +0x29 from each frame?
options: To make the output file smaller on disk
Because perf records the wrong offsets
Because flamegraph.pl cannot parse hexadecimal
So samples at different instructions in the same function merge into one stack line
explain: Two samples in convolve usually hit different instructions. With offsets kept they would be different stacks and the graph would split one function into many slivers. The script's header says offsets are stripped and identical stacks are coalesced with their counts summed.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
question: Which statement about the persistence domain on an ADR platform is correct?
options: Data is durable once the store instruction retires
Data is durable only once the 3D XPoint media has finished writing it
Data is durable once it reaches the memory controller's write pending queue
Data is durable once another core has read the new value
explain: ADR includes the WPQ: anything that reaches it is drained to the media on power failure. Retirement and visibility to other cores both happen while the line is still in a volatile cache. Waiting for the media itself is stronger than needed.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Why people are the most attacked surface
question: A company patches every server within a day of each release. Why does that not reduce its phishing risk much?
options: Phishing only works against unpatched browsers
Patching makes email filters less accurate
Phishing manipulates a person into using legitimate access, so no software flaw needs to exist
Phishing only targets home users, not companies
explain: A phish succeeds when a person types a password, approves a prompt or sends money through a normal process. Every step uses working software as designed, so patch speed barely matters. Malicious attachments can add a software exploit, but many phish need none.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Envelope, header and display name: why spoofing works
question: An email shows 'From: PayPal Security' on a phone. The underlying address is security@paypal-help.example and DMARC for paypal-help.example passes. What kind of spoof is this?
options: A display-name spoof combined with a lookalike domain the attacker owns
Exact-domain spoofing that DMARC failed to stop
A legitimate message, because DMARC passed
Envelope-from forgery only
explain: The attacker owns paypal-help.example, so authentication for that domain passes. The display name carries the deception. DMARC protects paypal.com's exact domain, not names that merely resemble it.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
question: An attacker sends from payroll.corp.example, a subdomain that does not exist in DNS. corp.example's record is 'v=DMARC1; p=reject; sp=none'. Without an np= tag, which policy applies?
options: reject, from p=
quarantine by default
No policy; non-existent domains are skipped
none, from sp=
explain: RFC 9989: if np= is absent, the sp= policy (if present) applies to non-existent subdomains, otherwise p=. Here that is none, so the spoof is delivered. Adding np=reject closes this gap, as gov.uk does.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and why passkeys resist it
question: Why can't an AiTM proxy simply forward a passkey login the same way?
options: Passkeys are too long to forward
The browser binds the credential to the site's domain and signs the real origin, so the proxy's domain gets no usable credential or a signature the server rejects
Passkeys only work offline
The proxy cannot read HTTPS traffic
explain: The proxy terminates HTTPS itself, so it can read traffic. What it cannot do is make the browser use a corp.example credential on its own domain, or change the signed origin. That is origin binding.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Alignment: which addresses a type is allowed to start at
question: A colleague says: "`char buf[8]; int *p = (int *)(buf + 1); *p = 7;` is fine on x86 because x86 allows unaligned loads." What is the best response?
options: The store is fine but the cast itself is a compile error
Correct, the cast is only a problem on ARM
In C this is undefined behavior regardless of the CPU; copy with memcpy instead
It is fine as long as buf is a global
explain: The C standard makes a misaligned pointer conversion undefined behavior, so the compiler may emit instructions that assume alignment (for example vector loads, single instructions that move 16 or more bytes at once and may require an aligned address). `memcpy` into an `int` is the portable way to read bytes at any address.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Overriding the rules: packed, alignas and unaligned data
question: Which is the right tool to give each of 8 per-thread counters its own 64-byte region in a static array?
options: __attribute__((packed)) on the counter struct
Casting the array to char *
Sorting the fields by alignment
alignas(64) on the counter field (or Rust #[repr(align(64))])
explain: Raising the alignment to 64 makes sizeof a multiple of 64, so every array element starts on a 64-byte boundary. Packing does the opposite and reordering cannot add space.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
question: Why is `size_of::<Option<Box<u8>>>()` equal to 8 on a 64-bit target?
options: Option is always pointer-sized
The compiler stores None in a global table
u8 has alignment 1, so the tag fits inside it
Box is never null, so null encodes None and no tag byte is needed
explain: Box<U> is in the std::option list of types where Option<T> has the same size as T. Option is not always pointer-sized: Option<u64> is 16 bytes.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
question: Two models both miss every keypoint by 6 px on the same people. Model A's errors are on the face; model B's are on hips and knees. Which has higher OKS?
options: Model A, faces are small so errors matter less
They are equal, since distances are equal
Model B, because hips and knees have larger sigma so the same distance is penalized less
It depends only on the person's area
explain: With the same d and s, the similarity depends on kappa. Hip and knee sigmas (.107, .087) are three to four times the face sigmas (.025 to .035), so B keeps much higher similarities.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Five families, one competition and two spectacular breaks
question: SIKE was broken in 2022. What did the attack require?
options: A quantum computer with a few thousand qubits
Only an ordinary computer: the final paper reports about ten minutes on one core for SIKEp434
Access to the victim's random number generator
A timing side channel on the decapsulating server
explain: Castryck and Decru's attack is a classical mathematical key recovery that uses the extra information in SIDH public keys. It needed no special access, which is why it ended SIKE rather than just one implementation.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Using ML-KEM correctly in code
question: A protocol needs separate keys for each direction from one ML-KEM shared secret. What is the right approach?
options: Derive each key with HKDF (or another approved KDF) using a distinct label such as 'client to server v1'
Split the 32 bytes into two 16-byte keys
Use the 32-byte secret for both directions
Encrypt the secret with itself
explain: FIPS 203 says further keys shall be derived in an approved way (SP 800-108 or SP 800-56C). Distinct labels give independent keys and bind each to its purpose.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Rolling it out: browsers, middleboxes and big certificates
question: Why did browsers take years to turn on post-quantum key agreement by default?
options: ML-KEM was too slow for browsers
Some middleboxes and servers assumed the ClientHello fits in one packet and failed on the larger hybrid one instead of falling back
Certificate authorities refused to issue ML-KEM certificates
TLS 1.3 had no way to negotiate new groups
explain: TLS already negotiates groups cleanly; buggy implementations broke that. Cloudflare estimates Chrome would have ramped up about five years earlier without these compatibility issues. ML-KEM is actually fast.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
question: Which query is the best fit for pre-filtering followed by a flat scan?
options: 50 million vectors, filter language = en matching 60% of them
2 million vectors, filter user_id = 42 matching 800 vectors
2 million vectors, no filter at all
50 million vectors, filter year > 2000 matching 90% of them
explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching vector. 800 distances is trivial and exact. The other cases would scan millions of vectors, where a graph search touches only a small fraction.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
question: A core keeps 16 lines in flight and memory latency rises from 80 ns to 120 ns. Peak DRAM bandwidth is not the limit. What happens to this core's bandwidth?
options: It stays at 12.8 GB/s because peak bandwidth did not change
It drops to about 8.5 GB/s
It rises, because longer latency means more lines are in flight
It drops to 0.8 GB/s
explain: With concurrency capped at 16 lines, $B = 16 \times 64 / 120 \approx 8.53$ GB/s. Little's law says bandwidth is concurrency divided by latency, so longer latency at fixed concurrency means less bandwidth.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
question: A fitness app encrypts all routes, has no breaches, and starts using routes to set prices for a partner insurer without telling users. Which NIST privacy engineering objective is most directly violated?
options: Confidentiality, because the data left the app
Predictability, because users cannot reliably anticipate this use of their data
Availability, because users lose control of their routes
Integrity, because the routes were changed
explain: Nothing was disclosed to an unauthorised party and nothing was altered or made unavailable. The problem is a use people could not anticipate: predictability. Confidentiality is a security objective about unauthorised access, and the insurer use here is authorised by the operator.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Location traces and aggregate maps: Strava 2018
question: de Montjoye and colleagues found that four hourly, antenna-level points identify 95 percent of people. What does coarsening the location resolution do?
options: Makes traces anonymous after one step
Reduces uniqueness only slowly, roughly as the 1/10 power of the resolution
Increases uniqueness
Has no effect
explain: The paper reports uniqueness decaying approximately as the 1/10 power of resolution: coarser data helps, but not enough on its own. That is why location needs stronger tools than rounding.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
question: An analyst asks for the same noisy count 100 times, each at epsilon = 0.1, and averages the answers. What is the privacy cost?
options: 0.1, because it is the same question
10, because composition adds the epsilons
0.001, because averaging reduces noise
Zero, because the answers are noisy
explain: Each independent noisy answer spends 0.1; 100 of them spend 10. Averaging improves accuracy exactly because it removes the protection. Serve repeats from a cache instead.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Privacy threat modelling with LINDDUN
question: Why is non-repudiation a threat in LINDDUN when it is a security goal in STRIDE?
options: LINDDUN disagrees with STRIDE about logging
Because for users, undeniable evidence of what they did or said can harm them, for example read receipts or signed records of a vote
Because non-repudiation requires encryption
Because GDPR forbids audit logs
explain: Evidence that protects a system (an admin audit log) can harm an individual where deniability matters. The designer decides per flow which property applies.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy
question: An attacker emails support from a lookalike address asking for 'all data you hold about me' for a victim's account. What control matters most?
options: Encrypting the export
Verifying the requester's identity in proportion to the data, for example by requiring the request from the authenticated account
Replying within one month
Deleting the data instead
explain: The risk is disclosure to an impostor. Proportionate identity verification (the ICO allows asking for information needed to confirm identity) and delivery to a verified channel prevent it; encryption does not help if you send it to the attacker.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 3: setuid, capabilities, kernel bugs, docker group
question: A contractor's account is in the docker group but has no sudo rights. How should an access review classify it?
options: Unprivileged: no sudo means no root
Root-equivalent: the docker group can start containers that write the host filesystem as root
Low risk unless the account also has a password
Privileged only inside containers
explain: Docker's own documentation says the docker group grants root-level privileges, because the root daemon will mount the host filesystem into a container on request. Review it exactly like a sudo ALL rule.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Credentials are the real currency: where they live on a host
question: An intruder has code running as an ordinary user on a laptop, with no admin rights yet. Which store can they most likely read immediately?
options: LSASS memory
The SAM hive
The user's browser password store
Other users' SSH keys
explain: Browser stores have traditionally been decrypted with the user's own logon credentials, so code running as that user can read them (Chrome's newer App-Bound Encryption, starting with cookies, raises that bar). LSASS and SAM need admin or SYSTEM, and other users' home directories are normally not readable.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Pivoting and tunnelling: reaching networks you cannot reach
question: Why does protocol tunnelling not make the activity invisible to network defenders?
options: Tunnels are always unencrypted
The outer connection still shows its endpoints, timing, duration and volume
Firewalls decrypt all SSH traffic by default
Tunnels only work over UDP
explain: Encapsulation hides the inner protocol, not the outer flow. A web server holding a long SSH session to an unusual host, or moving steady traffic for hours, stands out in flow and firewall logs without any decryption.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Step labels without humans: Monte Carlo rollouts
question: You double the number of rollouts per step from 8 to 16 to 'make the labels more accurate', using hard estimation. Which error grows?
options: Correct steps labeled bad, because more rollouts mean more failures
Wrong steps labeled good, because more rollouts give a lucky recovery more chances to occur
Neither; HE labels converge to the truth as N grows
Both shrink equally
explain: HE marks a step good if any rollout succeeds. P(at least one recovery) = 1 - (1-r)^N rises with N, so wrong steps get marked good more often. Correct-step false negatives (1-q)^N fall. Math-Shepherd observed exactly this: larger N led to false positives.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
question: Which of these was NOT one of DeepSeek-R1's stated reasons for not using a PRM in large-scale RL?
options: Defining a fine-grained step in general reasoning is hard
Judging intermediate-step correctness is hard, and manual labels do not scale
A model-based PRM leads to reward hacking and retraining adds overhead
PRMs cannot rerank top-N responses or assist guided search
explain: DeepSeek-R1 says the opposite: PRMs show good ability to rerank top-N responses and assist guided search. Their objection was that the benefit in large-scale RL did not outweigh the extra compute and complexity.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: A process's life: exec, exit, wait, zombies and orphans
question: A service holds a database connection on file descriptor 7, then runs an untrusted helper with `fork()` plus `execve()`. Which statement is true?
options: The helper inherits fd 7, still open, unless it was marked close-on-exec, so the helper can use the connection
execve() closes every descriptor except 0, 1 and 2
fd 7 is open in the helper but refers to a fresh copy of the socket
The helper cannot see fd 7 because execve() gives it a new PID
explain: execve() keeps the PID and keeps descriptors open by default; only those marked FD_CLOEXEC are closed. Mark sensitive descriptors close-on-exec when you open them, or close them in the child before exec.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
question: A CPU-bound image service runs 64 worker threads on an 8-core machine. `nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches` climbs by thousands per second per thread, and p99 latency (the time that 99 percent of requests finish within) is high even though CPU is at 100 percent. What is the best first change?
options: Add more worker threads so each request is more likely to find one free
Cut the pool to about 8 workers and queue requests, so each runs to completion on a core
Raise the time slice so involuntary switches become voluntary
Move the workers into separate processes for isolation
