explain: There are 8 times more runnable threads than cores, so threads keep preempting each other: high involuntary counts and late completions, as in the timeline. A core-sized pool with a queue removes most switches. Processes would make each switch more expensive, not rarer.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
question: Why does IVFADC build a new lookup table for each probed list instead of one table per query?
options: Each list has its own PQ codebook
The codes are encoded relative to that list's coarse centroid, so the query residual x - qc changes per list
Faiss recomputes tables to avoid cache misses
The table depends on the database vector id
explain: The stored codes describe y - qc(y). To compare, the query must be expressed relative to the same centroid, x - qc. The codebook is shared across lists, but the query sub-vectors differ, so the m x k* distances differ.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
question: You want to tune both the instruction and the demos of each predictor, your metric returns only a number (no textual feedback), and you have a moderate budget. Which optimizer do the DSPy docs point to?
options: LabeledFewShot
KNNFewShot
BootstrapFinetune
MIPROv2
explain: MIPROv2 searches instructions and demos jointly with Bayesian optimization and treats the metric as a black-box scalar. GEPA is the other strong option but gets most of its power from textual feedback in the metric; LabeledFewShot and KNNFewShot only choose demos; BootstrapFinetune changes weights.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: A residue is a rigid frame: rotation plus translation
question: You rotate an entire generated protein by 90 degrees about the z axis. What happens to the frames?
options: Every frame's rotation is left-multiplied by the same rotation and every translation is rotated; the protein is unchanged in substance
Only the translations change; the rotations are stored in local coordinates and are unaffected
Only the rotations change; CA positions are absolute and never move
The frames become invalid because the columns of R are no longer orthonormal
explain: A global rigid motion acts on every frame identically: each R becomes (global R) times R and each x becomes (global R) x plus the translation. The protein itself is the same object, which is exactly the symmetry an SE(3) model is built to respect.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
question: Line 10 of count_failed.py is changed to `if "failed" in line:`. What does the script print for the same five lines?
options: failed logins: 4
failed logins: 5
An error, because in only works on lists
failed logins: 0
explain: `in` is case-sensitive. The lines contain `Failed` with a capital F, never `failed`, so nothing matches and the count is 0. Use `"failed" in line.lower()` when you want a case-insensitive check. `in` works on strings as well as lists.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
question: Your script reports "0 matches" after hashing every file on a server against 20,000 SHA-256 IOCs from a vendor feed. What can you honestly conclude?
options: The server is clean
The feed must be broken
The attacker used MD5 instead
None of the files is an exact copy of a listed file
explain: Hash matching only detects byte-identical copies. Recompiled, repacked or slightly edited malware has a different hash, and so do files the feed never saw. Report what you actually tested.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
question: Which call is safe when `domain` comes from an alert?
options: subprocess.run(f"whois {domain}", shell=True)
subprocess.run("whois " + domain, shell=True)
os.system("whois " + domain)
subprocess.run(["whois", domain], timeout=30)
explain: Only the list form avoids the shell. The two shell=True strings and os.system all pass the text to /bin/sh, where a semicolon or backtick in domain starts a new command. Validating domain against a strict pattern is still a good second layer.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
question: Why does Rocchio usually set gamma much smaller than beta?
options: Nonrelevant documents are rare, so their centroid is unstable
Manning et al. report positive feedback is much more valuable than negative feedback
A large gamma makes the query vector longer, which BM25 penalizes
gamma must equal 1 - beta for the vector to stay normalized
explain: Relevant documents tend to resemble each other; nonrelevant ones are scattered across many topics, so subtracting their centroid says little. Some systems allow only positive feedback, which is gamma = 0.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Rewrite-Retrieve-Read: training a rewriter on the reader's feedback
question: In Rewrite-Retrieve-Read with RL, which components receive gradient updates?
options: The retriever and the rewriter
Only the reader
Only the small rewriter; the retriever and reader are frozen
All three, end to end
explain: The retriever (web search) and the reader (a black-box LLM API) are frozen. The design point is that a small trainable module in front adapts the query to them, using the reader's answer quality as the reward.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
question: Two 1024-bit codes have Hamming distance 312. What is the dot product of the corresponding +1/-1 sign vectors?
explain: Dot = D - 2H = 1024 - 624 = 400. Each of the 712 agreeing positions adds +1 and each of the 312 differing positions adds -1: 712 - 312 = 400.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
question: RaBitQ quantizes the query to 4-bit integers. What does it gain, and why is it safe?
options: It shrinks the index 4x; safe because queries are not stored
It makes the estimator exact; safe because rounding is random
It removes the need for the rotation
It turns the per-vector float dot product into a few AND plus popcount passes; safe because the added error is much smaller than the estimator's own O(1/sqrt(D)) error
explain: The code is already a 1-bit approximation, so computing its inner product in full float precision is overkill. Theorem 3.3 shows Theta(log log D) query bits keep the added error at the same order, and 4 bits made it negligible in the paper's tests.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Workflows as state machines: skipping, repeating and reordering steps
question: A password reset has three steps: request, enter emailed code, set new password. The set-password endpoint only checks that a `reset_user` value exists in the session. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, because the session is server-side
The emailed code can be brute forced faster
The code step can be skipped: after step 1, a request straight to step 3 sets the password without the code
The new password might be too short
explain: Step 1 put reset_user in the session, so step 3 accepts the request even though step 2 (proving control of the email) never happened. Step 3 must check that the session's reset is in the code-verified state, not just that it exists.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Case: Flexcoin and Poloniex, the bitcoin banks that raced (2014)
question: Flexcoin's flaw was in transfers between its own users. Why did that let the attacker take coins from the hot wallet?
options: Because internal transfers sent coins on the bitcoin network
Because the hot wallet keys were stored in user accounts
Because withdrawals pay out against internal balances, so inflated balances became real withdrawals
Because cold storage was empty
explain: Internal transfers only change numbers in Flexcoin's database, but those numbers decide how much each user may withdraw. Overdrawing the sender while crediting the receiver created balances backed by nothing, which the withdrawal system then paid out of the hot wallet.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Hidden sub-states: Kettle's GitLab email race (CVE-2022-4037)
question: Kettle's GitLab invitation probe returned one success, five "already taken" errors and two emails when sent in parallel, but six successes and one email when sent one by one. What does this tell a tester?
options: Nothing, error responses under load are normal
The server is rate limiting the tester
The deviation from the sequential baseline is a clue to a hidden sub-state worth investigating, even though no exploit is visible yet
Invitations are processed by PHP's session lock
explain: Kettle's method is to benchmark sequential behaviour first and treat any deviation under parallel load (different responses, extra emails, odd timing) as a clue. Two emails from mostly failed requests means some step ran twice. Without the baseline, the five errors would have looked normal.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
question: Server S2 is a follower with currentTerm 4. It receives RequestVote from S4 for term 3. What does S2 do?
options: Grants the vote if it has not voted yet in term 3
Rejects it and replies with term 4, so S4 learns it is behind
Becomes a candidate for term 5
Adopts term 3 and grants the vote
explain: Any request with a stale term is rejected, and the reply carries the responder's current term. When S4 sees term 4 it updates its term and returns to follower. Terms never go backward.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
question: A team fine-tunes an LLM on their product docs every quarter. Docs change weekly, and users need links to the source page. What does RAG give them that fine-tuning does not?
options: Higher fluency, because retrieved text improves the model's grammar
Fresh facts by re-indexing without retraining, and provenance because the answer can cite the retrieved chunk
Lower latency, because retrieval is always faster than generation
Nothing; fine-tuning and RAG update knowledge in the same way
explain: The index is non-parametric memory: changing it changes what the model can see, as the hot-swap experiment showed (68% vs 4% on 2018 leaders, with the 2018 vs the 2016 index). And because the evidence is an explicit chunk, the answer can point to it. Retrieval adds a step, so it does not lower latency.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
question: Your RAG chatbot gives wrong answers on 20% of test questions. On those, context recall averages 0.95 and faithfulness 0.55. Where should you work first?
options: The chunker: chunks are too small
Top-k: retrieve more chunks
The generation side: the right facts are in context but the answers make unsupported claims
The embedding model: retrieval is missing facts
explain: Context recall near 1 says the evidence is reaching the prompt. Faithfulness of 0.55 says nearly half the statements are not supported by it. That points at the prompt, the context noise, or the model, not at retrieval.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
question: You compute title BM25 for one document using IDF from the body field because it is already cached. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, IDF is a property of the term
Terms that are common in bodies but rare in titles get far too little weight in the title feature
The score becomes negative
Coverage stops working
explain: IDF depends on the field's own document frequencies. In the toy, fast has IDF 0.875 in titles but 0.087 in bodies. Using body IDF would make a title match on fast look almost worthless.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
question: A query has R = 3 relevant documents and your system ranks all 3 at the top. What is its P@10?
options: 1.0, since the ranking is perfect
0.3, since P@10 is capped at R/k
0.1, since only the first one counts
Undefined, since R is less than k
explain: P@10 divides hits by 10 no matter how many relevant documents exist, so 3/10 = 0.3 is the best possible. This is why P@k averaged over queries partly measures how many relevant documents each query has. R-precision (P@3 here) would give 1.0.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Implementation gotchas: ties, ideals, missing queries
question: Your new dense retriever scores 0.20 nDCG@10 lower than BM25 on an old TREC collection, and Judged@10 for it is 0.55 (BM25: 0.95). What should you conclude?
options: The dense retriever is clearly worse
Switch to exponential gain to fix the gap
Use MRR instead, which ignores unjudged documents
Nothing reliable yet: 45% of its top 10 is unjudged and counted as nonrelevant, so its score is a lower bound; judge those documents or report with judged_only
explain: Old qrels were pooled from old systems. Unjudged documents count as nonrelevant, which systematically penalizes a system that retrieves different documents. Low Judged@k is a warning that the comparison is biased, not evidence that the system is bad. MRR treats unjudged documents the same way.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Extortion layers: encryption, theft, leak sites and pressure
question: An analyst counts victims on a group's leak site to estimate how many organisations it attacked last month. Why is this estimate unreliable?
options: Groups like LockBit list only victims who refused to pay, and publication can lag the attack by months
Leak sites list victims only after payment
Leak sites are always fake
Leak sites only list victims outside the US
explain: CISA's LockBit advisory says leak sites show only the portion of victims who did not pay, and that publication dates can be months after the attack. Leak sites are real evidence, just incomplete and delayed.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Kaseya VSA and REvil, July 2021: one tool, many victims
question: Which change would fix the fail-open pattern in the model?
options: Add another elif comparing against a third hash
Hash the empty password before comparing
Make the final else return False and require a positive match to return True
Log failed logins
explain: Fail-closed means that the only way to succeed is to pass a check; everything else, including missing input, is denied. Adding comparisons keeps the permissive default; logging detects but does not prevent.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: The ransom decision: negotiation, proof of life and sanctions
question: Since 7 May 2024, why is a payment to a LockBit affiliate a much larger legal risk for a US company?
options: Cryptocurrency payments became illegal in the US
The UK ban applies to US companies
The FBI must approve every ransom payment
LockBit's leader is designated by the US Treasury, and payments reaching a designated person can violate OFAC rules on a strict liability basis
explain: Under LockBit's model the affiliate receives the ransom and sends the core its cut (lesson 1), so part of any payment reaches the designated leader. OFAC rules prohibit dealings with designated persons on a strict liability basis; cooperation with law enforcement is a mitigating factor. US law does not ban cryptocurrency or require FBI approval, and the UK announcement does not bind US firms.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: A peer's RDMA WRITE targets `remote_addr = 0x15040` in the 8-page region starting at `0x10000` (4 KB pages). Which page index and byte offset does the NIC write?
options: Page 4, offset 0x40
Page 5, offset 0x400
Page 5, offset 64
Page 21, offset 64
explain: Offset = 0x15040 - 0x10000 = 0x5040 = 20544 bytes. 20544 / 4096 = 5 remainder 64. So page index 5 at byte 64 (0x40). Page 21 comes from forgetting to subtract the base.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: A 64-node cluster with 24 threads per node uses one RC QP between every pair of threads. Using FaRM's formula, how many QPs does each machine hold, and what is the likely symptom?
options: 2 x 64 x 24 = 3072; none, QPs are free
64 x 24 = 1536; the CQ overflows
24 x 24 = 576; RNR errors
2 x 64 x 24 x 24 = 73,728; throughput drops from QP-state cache misses on the NIC
explain: 2mt squared = 2 x 64 x 576 = 73,728. QP state lives in host memory with the NIC caching it; FaRM saw request rates fall as the cluster grew for exactly this reason. One QP per thread per machine (3072) or sharing among q threads cuts it.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
question: A racing game with heavy, fast cars shows remote cars stuttering. Which technique fits best before adding interpolation delay?
options: Dead reckoning from last known speed and heading, corrected by each update
Lag compensation
Server reconciliation of remote cars
Masking WebSocket frames
explain: A fast car cannot change direction instantly, so its position is predictable from speed and heading: the classic case for dead reckoning. Lag compensation is about hit tests; reconciliation applies to your own inputs.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Matrix factorization: learning user and item vectors
question: You have billions of implicit events (every user-item pair counts) and a cluster of machines. Which optimizer do Koren et al. suggest, and why?
options: SGD, because it is always faster than ALS
Neither; matrix factorization cannot use implicit data
SGD with a larger learning rate, to make up for the dense data
ALS, because each user (and each item) vector is an independent least-squares solve that parallelizes, and it avoids looping over every cell of a dense matrix
explain: Both reasons are stated in the paper: ALS parallelizes naturally, and for implicit data the training set is not sparse, so per-cell SGD loops are impractical. Hu et al. show how ALS stays linear in the number of non-zeros.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
question: Your new model beats matrix factorization on a random 80/20 holdout of watch events. Before shipping, what is the most important check?
options: Re-run with a different random seed for the same 80/20 split
Evaluate with a temporal split (train on the past, predict later events) against tuned baselines, then A/B test
Switch the metric from recall@k to RMSE
Add more epochs until offline recall stops improving
explain: A random holdout lets the model see a user's future and future popularity. A temporal split matches deployment, tuned simple baselines guard against weak comparisons (Dacrema et al.), and only an online test measures the real effect.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Three ways to join two tables
question: The outer side of a join yields 10 rows after a filter. The inner table has 10000 rows and a B-tree index on the join key. Which plan is most likely cheapest?
options: Nested loop with an index scan on the inner side
Hash join, building on the 10000-row table
Merge join after sorting both sides
Nested loop with a sequential scan of the inner side
explain: Ten index lookups touch only a few pages each, while a hash join must read all 10000 inner rows once. The PostgreSQL docs show exactly this case (unique1 < 10) choosing Nested Loop with an inner Index Scan. A nested loop with a sequential inner scan would read the 10000-row table 10 times.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
question: A web app writes a profile update to the primary, then immediately reads it from a synchronous standby configured with `synchronous_commit = on`. Users sometimes see the old profile. Why?
options: The standby is asynchronous despite the setting
Synchronous replication only applies to DDL (data definition language: schema-changing) statements
The standby flushed the WAL record but had not yet replayed it when the read arrived
The primary acknowledged before flushing its own WAL
explain: `on` waits for the standby to flush the commit record to disk, not to apply it. Replay is a separate step, so a read can arrive in between. `remote_apply` closes that gap at a higher commit latency, or the app can read its own writes from the primary.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
question: Vector clocks: version X = [(Sx,3),(Sy,1)] and version Y = [(Sx,2),(Sy,2)]. What should a Dynamo-style store do on a read that finds both?
options: Return both as concurrent siblings
Keep X, since Sx's counter is larger
Keep Y, since it has the larger total
Keep whichever has the later wall-clock timestamp
explain: X is ahead on Sx (3 vs 2) but behind on Sy (1 vs 2), so neither descends from the other. They are concurrent, and the store returns both for reconciliation. Picking by one counter, a sum or a wall clock would silently drop an update.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: What RLHF reward hacking looks like: length, sycophancy, persuasion
question: A judge's fitted length-controlled model gives your model theta = 0.4. Its raw win rate is 80 percent and its answers are much longer than the baseline's. What is its LC win rate?
options: 80 percent: length control only matters for shorter answers
50 percent: length control resets every model to even
40 percent: theta read as a probability
About 60 percent: the logistic of 0.4, the predicted win rate at equal length
explain: Setting the length difference to 0 leaves sigma(theta) = 1/(1 + e^-0.4), about 0.599. Theta is a log-odds, not a probability, and LC does not reset models to 50 percent: only a model as good as the baseline at equal length gets 50.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
question: A team evaluates a support agent on 500 single-turn prompts and finds no policy violations. In production the agent retries after API errors and sees its earlier messages. What does Pan et al. (2024) suggest?
options: The result transfers, since the weights are identical
Strengthen the system prompt and ship
Evaluate with multi-step feedback loops and injected errors, because ICRH grows with cycles of feedback that a static evaluation never runs
Switch to a larger model
explain: ICRH is a feedback-loop phenomenon: violations grew with rounds of error feedback in ToolEmu. A single-turn test runs zero cycles. The paper found larger models sometimes worse and better-specified prompts unlikely to fix it.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Putting money on risk: ALE and the FAIR model
question: Laptop theft: asset value USD 1,500, exposure factor 1.0, about 4 thefts a year. A control costs USD 5,000 a year and halves the theft rate. Based on ALE alone, is it worth it?
options: Yes, it saves USD 6,000 a year
Yes, any control that halves risk is worth it
No: ALE falls from USD 6,000 to 3,000, saving USD 3,000 for USD 5,000
Cannot compute without FAIR
explain: SLE = 1,500; ALE = 1,500 x 4 = 6,000; with the control ALE = 3,000. Saving 3,000 a year for 5,000 a year loses money, unless the laptops hold data whose breach costs more, which would change the SLE.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
question: A company excludes Annex A control 7.4 (physical security monitoring) in its SoA. When is that acceptable?
options: Never; all 93 controls are mandatory
When the exclusion is justified, for example no premises in scope and the cloud provider's physical controls are covered elsewhere
Only if the CEO signs it
Only in the first year of certification
explain: Clause 6.1.3 d) requires justification for excluding Annex A controls. A justified exclusion is fine; an unjustified one is a nonconformity.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Compliance as code: policy checks in CI and automatic evidence
question: The plan check passes, but an engineer later disables encryption on a bucket by hand in the AWS console. What catches it?
options: Nothing can catch it
A live-configuration check (for example an AWS Config rule) or the nightly evidence snapshot, plus Terraform drift detection
The same plan check on the next pull request, always
The SOC 2 report
explain: Plan checks see only changes made through Terraform. Manual changes need detection on the live account: config rules, scheduled snapshots, or terraform plan showing drift.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Policies people follow and awareness that works
question: An auditor finds the policy says 'all laptops use full-disk encryption' but the device report shows 7 percent unencrypted. Which response best fixes the problem?
options: Change the policy to 'most laptops'
Enforce encryption through device management so unencrypted laptops cannot reach company systems, record exceptions for the rest with expiry dates, and keep the device report as evidence
Send a reminder email
Remove the policy
explain: Make the system enforce the rule, handle real exceptions explicitly, and let the enforcement produce evidence. Rewording or reminders leave the gap open.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: In the toy model, the 16,000-token response is replaced by one of 4000 tokens. What happens to the synchronous rollout time?
options: It drops to 80 s, because every engine now finishes at 4000 tokens
It drops from 320 s to 122 s, because engine 3's 6100-token response becomes the longest
It stays at 320 s, because the batch size is unchanged
It drops to about 79 s, the mean length times 20 ms
explain: A synchronous batch ends when its longest response ends. Without the 16k response the longest is 6100 tokens on engine 3, so 6100 x 20 ms = 122 s. The mean sets throughput only if nothing waits for the tail.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: Your synchronous colocated run spends 80% of each step in rollout, and one response in each batch runs to the 32k cap. Which plan addresses the root cause with the least algorithmic risk first?
options: Fully async with staleness 16 and no importance correction
Add training GPUs
Partial rollouts or a one-step overlap with bounded staleness and decoupled importance weights, then measure accuracy against a synchronous baseline
Lower the cap to 2k tokens
explain: The root cause is waiting on the long tail. Partial rollouts or a small, bounded staleness keep GPUs busy while keeping data nearly on-policy, and the decoupled objective corrects what remains. Large unbounded staleness risks learning quality; more trainers do not touch rollout; a tight cap truncates real reasoning.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: The four golden signals, read as distributions
question: Which single measurement best distinguishes the hypothesis that catalog is itself saturated from the hypothesis that catalog's database got slow?
options: Catalog's p99 latency, which is 1000 ms either way
Catalog's error rate of 7.41 percent
The number of catalog pods firing alerts
Catalog's pool wait time against its database query time: 988 ms waiting for a connection versus 12 ms executing the query
explain: p99, error rate and alert count are identical under both hypotheses, so none of them discriminates. Splitting the latency into time spent waiting for a resource and time spent doing work does: the query still takes 12 ms, so the database is fine and the backlog is in front of the pool. Instrument the wait and the work separately, or you cannot tell these apart during an incident.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
question: Your organisation writes excellent postmortems and the same class of incident keeps recurring. Which measurement would tell you where the process is leaking?
options: Mean time to resolution for the recurring class
Number of postmortems written per quarter
The fraction of action items with an owner, a bug and a priority that were completed, broken down by type
Number of alerts fired per incident
explain: Writing the document is not the mechanism that reduces recurrence; completing the typed, owned, tracked items is. Counting postmortems measures effort, and MTTR measures response rather than prevention. If completion is low, the leak is in prioritisation; if completion is high and recurrence continues, the items are not naming the right conditions.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
question: You are writing a Rust driver and need a C function from a subsystem that has no Rust abstraction yet. What does kernel policy expect?
options: Call it through `bindings::` inside an `unsafe` block in the driver, with a SAFETY comment
Add (or extend) a safe abstraction for it in the subsystem's Rust code, and use that from the driver
Rewrite the C function in Rust inside the driver so no FFI is needed
Use `extern "C"` to declare the function by hand in the driver
explain: The general-information doc says leaf modules such as drivers should not use the C bindings directly; subsystems provide as-safe-as-possible abstractions. Declaring the symbol yourself is the same forbidden shortcut with less checking. Duplicating the C logic would create a second implementation to maintain.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Objects the C side owns: ARef, AlwaysRefCounted and RCU
question: A callback receives `t: &Task`. You want a work item to log that task's pid a few seconds later. What do you store in the work item?
options: `ARef::from(t)`: it takes a reference with get_task_struct and drops it with put_task_struct when the work item is dropped
`t` itself, as a `&'static Task` obtained with `core::mem::transmute`
`Arc::new(t)`, which shares the task between the callback and the work item
A bitwise copy of the C `task_struct`
explain: Only the ARef owns an increment of the task's real count. The transmuted reference compiles but nothing keeps the task alive: a use-after-free waiting to happen. `Arc::new(t)` would allocate a new object holding a borrowed `&Task` whose lifetime still ends with the callback, so it does not extend anything. Copying a task_struct copies pointers it does not own.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
question: Code under review creates `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` once to read and validate a header, then creates a second `UserSlice::new(arg, size).reader()` to read the whole request and use it. What is the problem?
options: It is a double fetch: user memory can change between the two readers, so the validated header is not the one being used
Nothing: `copy_from_user` re-validates the data on every call
It cannot compile, because a `UserSlice` can only be created once per address
The second reader starts where the first one stopped, so it misses the header
explain: Each reader consumes its own UserSlice and advances independently, so the second one starts at the beginning again. `copy_from_user` checks the *address range*, not the contents. The uaccess.rs docs show exactly this pattern labelled as a TOCTOU bug and advise one UserSlice per user memory block.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
X, because the global DSQ is consumed before ops.dispatch() is ever called
Y, because custom DSQs have priority over built-in ones
Neither until ops.dispatch() chooses between them
explain: The pick order is fixed: local DSQ, then global DSQ, then ops.dispatch(). X is taken from the global DSQ without consulting the BPF scheduler. Y only moves if ops.dispatch() later calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(7).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Placement and preemption: idle CPUs, kicks, LOCAL_ON and locality
question: Your enqueue inserts a task into custom DSQ 3 while CPU 5 is idle. Nothing kicks CPU 5, and the other CPUs never read DSQ 3 in their dispatch. What can happen?
options: CPU 5 polls custom DSQs and notices within one tick
The kernel moves custom DSQ tasks to the global DSQ after one slice
The task waits while CPU 5 stays idle, until some CPU happens to dispatch from DSQ 3 or the watchdog fires
The verifier rejects enqueue callbacks that do not kick a CPU
explain: An idle CPU runs the scheduling path only when it is woken: by select_cpu choosing it, by a kick, or by new work in its local DSQ. Custom DSQs are only read by dispatch callbacks, so an unread queue plus no kick leaves the task stranded.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
question: After loading your scheduler, SCX_EV_SELECT_CPU_FALLBACK in /sys/kernel/sched_ext/root/events climbs steadily. What does it point to?
options: The scheduler keeps entering bypass mode
Tasks are being inserted without a slice
Your select_cpu returns CPUs the tasks cannot use, and the core silently picks another one
The watchdog is about to declare a stall
explain: The kernel docs define it as ops.select_cpu() returning a CPU unusable by the task, after which the core picks a fallback. Look for a missing check against p->cpus_ptr, the task's allowed cpumask.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Revocation at scale: CircleCI and rotating every secret at once
question: A breach report says secrets were stolen on 22 December, and you finish rotating on 9 January. Which window do you search your own logs for misuse of those secrets?
options: Only 4 January, the disclosure date
From the earliest possible compromise (16 December here) until your rotation finished on 9 January
From 22 December onward
Only after 9 January
explain: Investigate the whole period a stolen copy could have worked: from the earliest date the vendor could not rule out until your rotation completed. CircleCI's own advice was 16 December through the date you rotated.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Key hierarchies in KMS: envelope encryption and rotating the KEK
question: Following Google's DEK guidance, how often should you rotate a DEK?
options: Every 90 days
Whenever the KEK rotates
Never in place: generate a new DEK every time you write the data, so each DEK protects one write
Only after a breach
explain: A fresh DEK per write means there is no long-lived DEK to rotate. KEK rotation does not touch DEKs at all unless you re-wrap them, and re-wrapping changes the wrapping, not the DEK itself.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Rotation without outages: overlap, versions and staged labels
question: In the overlap timeline, when is it safe to remove k1 from the verifiers' key set?
options: As soon as k2 is published
As soon as signing switches to k2
Once the last token signed with k1 has expired
Never; old keys must be kept forever
explain: Tokens signed by k1 keep arriving until they expire. Removing k1 earlier rejects valid tokens (an outage); keeping it forever means a stolen k1 works forever, which is the Storm-0558 failure.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: eval, pickle and yaml.load turn data into code
question: A service loads job descriptions from a shared message queue with `pickle.loads(msg.body)`. The queue is internal. What is the best review comment?
options: Fine: internal queues are trusted by definition
Anyone who can publish to the queue gets code execution in the worker; switch to JSON with a schema
Wrap the call in try/except so malformed messages do not crash the worker
Check isinstance(result, Job) after loading
explain: pickle runs code while loading, so whoever can write to the queue controls the worker. try/except and isinstance checks happen after the code already ran. Internal is not the same as trusted: a compromise of any producer would spread.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
question: You are reviewing a 2013-style patch that adds a new lookup type to a logging library. Which review comment best addresses the risk?
options: Add unit tests that the lookup returns the right value for a valid name
Lookups are evaluated on logged data, so this lets any logged string trigger a network fetch and code load; make it opt-in and never apply lookups to message data
Rename the plugin to make its purpose clearer
Document the new syntax in the README
explain: The danger is not that the lookup works incorrectly but that it works on attacker-controlled data. Tests of the happy path, naming and documentation do not address that. The CSRB said a focused security review of exactly this addition could have found the flaw.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Heartbleed as a diff: reviewing every field of a message
question: Why did Cloudflare's report say `>=` would have prevented Cloudbleed even though the grammar bug would still exist?
options: Because >= is faster than ==
Because a pointer that jumps past the end still satisfies p >= pe, so the parser stops instead of reading on
Because >= prevents the pointer from moving
Because Ragel only supports >=
explain: An equality check only fires if the pointer lands exactly on the end. If it skips over, == is never true. An ordering check is true for every position at or past the end, so it fails safe even when another bug moves the pointer too far.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Rust: FFI boundaries, release-mode overflow and panics
question: Which FFI call is correct for passing a Rust string to a C function that expects a NUL-terminated string?
options: `f(name.as_ptr() as *const c_char)` with `name: &str`
`let c = CString::new(name)?; unsafe { f(c.as_ptr()) }`
`unsafe { f(CString::new(name).unwrap().into_raw()) }` and never free it
`unsafe { f(name.to_string().as_ptr() as *const c_char) }`
explain: A &str or String has no terminating NUL, so C would read past its end. into_raw without a matching from_raw leaks memory, and unwrap panics on interior NULs. Binding the CString to a variable keeps it alive for the call and guarantees exactly one terminator.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Secure channels at every layer: what each protocol protects
question: An employee connects to the office through a VPN and then opens an old telnet session to a router inside the office. Who can read the telnet password?
options: Nobody, because the VPN encrypts the whole session end to end
Only the VPN provider, which can see inside the tunnel
Anyone who can capture traffic on the office network between the VPN gateway and the router
Nobody, because telnet hashes passwords before sending them
explain: The VPN protects only the stretch from the laptop to the gateway. After the gateway the telnet packets travel in the clear across the office network. SSH would protect the session all the way to the router. Telnet sends the password as typed; it does not hash it.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: IPsec traps: weak PSKs, aggressive mode, NULL and old algorithms
question: Which ESP setting is forbidden outright by RFC 4303?
options: AES-GCM with a 16-byte ICV
NULL encryption with HMAC-SHA-256 integrity
Both encryption and integrity set to NULL
Tunnel mode between two hosts
explain: RFC 4303 allows NULL encryption (integrity only) and, as a MAY, confidentiality-only ESP, but encryption and integrity "MUST NOT both be NULL". Tunnel mode between hosts is unusual but legal.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Terrapin (CVE-2023-48795): deleting SSH messages by shifting a counter
question: Why is a connection using aes256-gcm@openssh.com not affected by Terrapin?
options: AES-256 has a longer key than ChaCha20
GCM derives its nonce from a separate invocation counter, not from the shifted sequence number
GCM encrypts the IGNORE message so the attacker cannot inject it
GCM connections do not send EXT_INFO
explain: The attacker shifts the implicit sequence number. ChaCha20-Poly1305 and EtM MACs use it in their integrity check, so the shift is invisible. GCM's nonce starts from a key-derived value and counts invocations independently, so it does not line up after the shift.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Time is a security input: NTP, delay attacks and NTS
question: An attacker on the path between a client and its NTS server cannot break the cryptography. What can they still do to the client's clock?
options: Nothing, NTS makes time synchronisation fully secure
Replace the time in the reply with any value
Replay an old reply to set the clock back by days
Delay packets asymmetrically, shifting the computed offset by up to half the round-trip delay
explain: Delays leave packets authentic, so NTS cannot detect them; the offset error is bounded by half the round trip (MAXDIST/2 at most). Rewriting the time or replaying old replies fails NTS's authentication and request-response matching.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: What security architecture is: where every control sits
question: A team adds a GraphQL endpoint that queries the database directly, while the REST routes all pass through the authorization middleware. Which reference monitor requirement does the new endpoint break?
options: Always invoked
Tamper proof
Small enough to analyse
Open design
explain: The middleware is a reference monitor, and the new endpoint reaches the objects without calling it. Tamper proofing is about attackers modifying the checker; size is about whether it can be reviewed; open design is a separate Saltzer and Schroeder principle.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Brewer-Nash's Chinese Wall, and choosing the right model
question: A hospital wants to ensure that prescription records change only through the pharmacy system's dispensing workflow, with a pharmacist approving what a doctor writes. Which model fits best?
options: Bell-LaPadula
Biba strict integrity
Brewer-Nash
Clark-Wilson
explain: The concern is how data changes: through certified programs (the dispensing workflow) with separation of duty (doctor writes, pharmacist approves). That is Clark-Wilson. Bell-LaPadula is about disclosure, Biba about trust levels, Brewer-Nash about conflicts of interest.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: NIST SP 800-207: the logical architecture of zero trust
question: During a session the policy engine learns that the device is infected and revokes access. Which component carries out that decision?
options: The policy engine itself, by blocking packets
The resource, by logging the user out
The policy administrator, by signalling the PEP to terminate the session
The SIEM, by alerting an analyst
explain: The PE decides and logs; the PA executes, including revoking an earlier approval by telling the PEP to shut the connection. The PEP is what actually terminates the traffic. A SIEM alert alone does not close anything.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Segmentation and microsegmentation, planned from real traffic
question: Why does SP 800-215 put a unique application identity first among microsegmentation prerequisites?
options: Because IP addresses change and are hidden by NAT, proxies, load balancers and moving VMs, so policy written on addresses cannot say which workload is talking
Because identities are cheaper to store than addresses
Because firewalls cannot read IP headers
Because SPIFFE is required by law
explain: Policy should say which workload may call which, and only a verifiable workload identity (such as a SPIFFE ID in a short-lived certificate) survives the address changes of modern infrastructure.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: From a script to a pipeline: the parts of a security automation
question: Enriching one alert takes about 40 seconds of API calls. Which component should do that work?
options: The receiver, before it answers the SIEM
A worker that takes the alert from the queue
The SIEM, before it sends the alert
The chat bot, when the analyst opens the case
explain: The receiver must answer fast (GitHub, for example, gives up after 10 seconds and counts the delivery as failed), so slow work belongs in workers behind the queue. Making the SIEM or chat bot do it couples your pipeline to tools you do not control.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
question: Why add jitter rather than using exponential backoff alone?
options: Jitter makes each retry faster
Without jitter the API will not accept the retry
Jitter replaces the need to honour Retry-After
Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together at every step, recreating the overload
explain: Exponential backoff with identical timing keeps failed clients in lock step. Randomising the wait spreads them out. Retry-After, when present, still sets the minimum wait.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Worked scenario: prompt injection through attacker-written log fields
question: Which change prevents the attacker from closing A-2291 even if the model is fully persuaded?
options: A stronger system prompt telling the model to ignore instructions in alerts
Blocking the phrase ignore previous instructions
Wrapping each field in its own XML tag
Removing the model's ability to close or downgrade alerts, with deterministic rules making those decisions
explain: Only removing the authority holds when the model is persuaded. Prompts and tags lower the odds (and the attacker can write the closing tag); phrase blocklists are rephrased around.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
question: A web shop's product prices are changed by an intruder so that a laptop sells for USD 1. Customers can still browse and buy, and no customer data was read. Which property was violated?
options: Integrity
Confidentiality
Availability
Non-repudiation
explain: The data was improperly modified, which is an integrity failure. Nothing secret was read (confidentiality held) and the shop stayed up (availability held). Non-repudiation is about proving who created data, which is not the issue here.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: How a vulnerability becomes public: disclosure, CVE and NVD
question: Why does the security world need CVE IDs at all?
options: They give every publicly known vulnerability one shared name that scanners, advisories and people can refer to
They encrypt vulnerability details so attackers cannot read them
They rate how dangerous a bug is
They prove the vendor has fixed the bug
explain: A CVE ID is an identifier, nothing more. Severity is CVSS's job, exploitation status is KEV's, and fix status comes from the vendor advisory. One name lets a scanner report, a vendor bulletin and a news story be matched up.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The attack lifecycle: kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK
question: In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
options: A tactic is the attacker's goal at that step; a technique is a specific way of achieving it
Tactics are for Windows, techniques for Linux
Tactics are legal, techniques are illegal
There is no difference; they are synonyms
explain: MITRE describes tactics as the why (for example Credential Access) and techniques as the how (for example T1552.001 Credentials In Files). One tactic has many techniques.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: What a security leader is for: the CISO's job and reporting line
question: A CISO reports to the CIO. The CIO's infrastructure team owns 40 unpatched internet-facing servers. What is the main governance risk of this reporting line here?
options: The CISO cannot technically scan the servers
The finding about the CIO's own systems may be softened or delayed before it reaches the CEO and board
The CIO is legally barred from fixing servers the CISO has flagged
Reporting to the CIO makes the CISO the owner of the risk
explain: The issue is a conflict of interest in the information path, not technical access. Risk ownership stays with the business or system owner under the Three Lines Model; a direct audit-committee channel is the usual remedy.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Prioritising a portfolio: expected loss removed per dollar
question: An option removes little expected loss per dollar but is required by a signed customer contract. What should happen?
options: Fund it as an obligation, and record why it sits outside the ranking
Drop it; ratios decide everything
Hide it in another line
Ask the customer to remove the clause before deciding
explain: Obligations are funded regardless of ratio, and the reason is recorded so the portfolio stays explainable. The ranking applies to discretionary spending.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Hiring and keeping people: what predicts performance
question: According to Sackett et al. (2022), which method had the highest mean validity?
options: Years of job experience
Structured interviews
Unstructured interviews
Cognitive ability tests
explain: Structured interviews (0.42) ranked first; cognitive ability tests (0.31) were lower than earlier estimates suggested; unstructured interviews (0.19) and years of experience (0.07) were weak.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Personal liability: what the Uber and SolarWinds records say
question: Which part of the SEC's SolarWinds case survived the July 2024 motion to dismiss?
options: Fraud claims based on the public Security Statement's access-control and password representations
Claims that weak cybersecurity violated internal accounting controls
Claims about the December 2020 8-Ks
Disclosure-controls claims
explain: The court sustained claims about the Security Statement and dismissed the others; in November 2025 the remaining claims were dismissed with prejudice by stipulation.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Severity you can defend: scores, context and confidence
question: A report says only: "Severity: 9.8". What is the most important thing missing?
options: Which scale and version produced it (for example CVSS 3.1 base) and whether it was adjusted for this environment
Nothing; 9.8 is clear
The colour of the severity badge
The name of the tester
explain: The CVSS 4.0 specification asks for nomenclature (CVSS-B, BT, BE, BTE) wherever a number appears, because the same bug scores differently by version and by which metric groups were used.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Incident updates when you do not know yet
question: Which incident update sentence best states uncertainty?
options: We judge it unlikely (about 30%) that customer data was accessed; this rests on 60% of logs reviewed, and we expect a firmer answer by 16:00.
The attacker definitely did not reach customer data.
Customer data may have potentially been impacted in some way.
We cannot comment during an investigation.
explain: It gives a word with a number, the basis for the judgement, and when it will improve. 'Definitely did not' overstates, 'may have potentially' is vague, and 'cannot comment' gives readers nothing to plan with.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions
question: Which slide title is best for a board?
options: Ransomware could stop order fulfilment for about 5 days; target 2; closing the gap needs the backup budget on today's agenda
Firewall dropped 4.2M packets from 37 countries
We are fully compliant with all frameworks
Top 10 CVEs this quarter
explain: It names a business outcome, a measured current state, a target and the decision needed. The others are activity, an unfalsifiable claim, or technical detail directors cannot act on.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
question: Your ReST-EM run uses 64 samples per problem, yet 20% of training problems never get a correct sample. Which change gives the model a training signal on exactly those problems?
options: Train for more epochs on the solutions you already kept
Lower the sampling temperature so solutions are more careful
Continue fine-tuning from the last checkpoint instead of the base model
STaR's rationalization: give the correct answer as a hint and keep rationales that reach it
explain: Problems with no correct sample are invisible to the filter; more training on kept data or lower temperature cannot add them. Rationalization samples from a different distribution, p(r | x, y), which can reach the answer. The cost, covered in lesson 5, is more rationales that reach the right answer for the wrong reasons.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Using failures and training the judge: V-STaR, the gap, Meta-Rewarding
question: What does V-STaR train on that STaR throws away?
options: Rationales produced with the answer given as a hint
Human-written solutions from the SFT set only
Preference labels from a stronger model
Incorrect self-generated solutions, paired with correct ones to train a DPO verifier
explain: STaR keeps only correct samples. V-STaR keeps every labeled sample in the verifier's data and builds pairs of correct and incorrect solutions to the same problem, so the verifier learns this generator's typical mistakes.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Why exact-match caches miss, and how a semantic cache matches meaning
question: A colleague sets RedisVL's distance_threshold to 0.2, thinking it is stricter than the default 0.1. What did they actually do?
options: Made it stricter: hits now need similarity of at least 0.98
Made it looser: hits now need only cosine similarity of at least 0.8
Nothing, because the threshold is ignored for short prompts
Switched from cosine to Euclidean distance
explain: It is a distance, so a larger value accepts neighbors that are farther away. d at most 0.2 means similarity at least 0.8. More hits, and more chances to return the answer to a different question.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Prompt compression: pruning tokens with a small language model
question: What is the main design difference between LLMLingua-2 and the original LLMLingua?
options: LLMLingua-2 uses GPT-4 at inference time to rewrite each prompt
LLMLingua-2 caches compressed prompts across users
LLMLingua-2 classifies each token as preserve or discard with a bidirectional encoder trained on GPT-4-distilled labels, instead of using a causal LM's perplexity
LLMLingua-2 only drops whole documents
explain: GPT-4 is used offline to create training labels, not at inference. The small encoder sees context on both sides of each token and is trained directly for the compression objective, which the paper credits for its speed and faithfulness.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
question: Your validator uses Python's urlsplit, and the fetch is done by a separate Node service that receives the original URL string. What is the most robust fix?
options: Add more characters to a denylist
Run both parsers and accept if either says the host is allowed
Have the validator pass on only the parsed, allowlisted host (or an ID) and let the fetcher build the URL itself from fixed parts
Lowercase the URL first
explain: When a URL string crosses a boundary and is parsed again, the two parsers can disagree. Passing structured, already-validated parts (or an identifier for an allowlisted destination) removes the second parse entirely.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Log4Shell response: versions, mitigations and detection
question: It is 15 December 2021. A Java 8 service runs Log4j 2.15.0, which you deployed in a hurry on 11 December. What should you do?
options: Upgrade to 2.16.0 or later, since 2.15.0 was found incomplete in some configurations (CVE-2021-45046), and keep egress filtering in place
Nothing: 2.15.0 fixed CVE-2021-44228
Downgrade to Log4j 1.x
Remove log4j-api and keep log4j-core
explain: CVE-2021-45046, published 14 December, showed 2.15.0 could still be exploited in some non-default configurations; 2.16.0 removed message lookups entirely. Log4j 1.x is end of life with its own issues, and log4j-core is the vulnerable part.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon
question: Which architecture change removes the classic Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding ambiguity?
options: Adding a second HTTP/1.1 proxy
Increasing the Content-Length limit
Speaking HTTP/2 from the client all the way to the back end
Turning on gzip compression
explain: HTTP/2 frames carry their own lengths, so there is one way to find a request's end. A front end that downgrades to HTTP/1.1 for the back end brings the ambiguity back, which is where newer variants live.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Compressed FSMs: decoding several tokens in one step
question: Why does SGLang retokenize after a jump instead of appending the jumped string's own tokens?
options: Retokenizing is the only way to compute logits
The jumped string has no tokens until the detokenizer runs
Tokenizing the jumped piece alone can give splits the model rarely saw (summa plus ry), shifting its next-token distribution; retokenizing keeps the context close to normal
To make the KV cache smaller
explain: Models are trained on canonical BPE tokenizations. A non-canonical boundary changes the input the model conditions on. The paper and blog retokenize the text to keep it aligned, at a small cost.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
question: What does A* do if h(n) = 0 for every node?
options: It settles exactly the nodes plain Dijkstra settles, since f = g
It fails, because 0 is not a valid lower bound
It settles only the nodes on the shortest path
It becomes breadth-first search
explain: Zero never overestimates, so it is admissible, but it gives no guidance: f equals g and the queue order is Dijkstra's. The paper notes this trivial estimate satisfies the consistency assumption.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The DFT: one dot product per complex sinusoid
question: x is a real signal of length 8 and its DFT has X[3] = 2 + 5i. What is X[5]?
options: 0, because only one of a pair can be nonzero
explain: For real input, X[N - k] is the complex conjugate of X[k]. Here N - 3 = 5, so X[5] = 2 - 5i. This symmetry is why rfft can skip the upper half of the bins without losing information.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: One instruction, many lanes: SIMD registers and lane counts
question: Which of these operations is horizontal rather than vertical?
options: out[i] = a[i] * b[i] for 8 lanes
out[i] = max(a[i], 0) for 8 lanes
Adding the 8 lanes of one register into a single total
Comparing a[i] > b[i] lane by lane
explain: A horizontal operation combines lanes of the same register. The other three only pair lane i with lane i, so they are vertical and cost one instruction each.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
question: Why can SVE vectorize strlen safely while a naive fixed-width SIMD strlen risks a crash?
options: SVE registers are wider
First-faulting loads record lanes that would fault in FFR instead of trapping
SVE checks string lengths in hardware
strlen is always auto-vectorized on Arm
explain: Reading a full vector past the terminating zero can cross into an unmapped page. ldff1 suppresses faults after the first active lane and marks which lanes loaded in FFR, so the loop processes only those and continues. Fixed-width code needs alignment tricks to avoid crossing pages.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The buddy allocator: split in halves, merge with one XOR
question: A free block of order 2 starts at pfn 12. Where is its buddy, and if the buddy is also free, where does the merged order-3 block start?
options: Buddy at pfn 16; merged block starts at 12
Buddy at pfn 14; merged block starts at 12
Buddy at pfn 8; merged block starts at 8
Buddy at pfn 4; merged block starts at 4
explain: 12 in binary is 1100. Order 2 means flip bit 2 (value 4): 1100 XOR 0100 = 1000 = 8. The merged block starts at 12 AND 8 = 8, and covers pfn 8 to 15. Note that 16 is wrong: 12 to 19 would not be aligned to 8.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
question: A colocated run runs out of GPU memory in SGLang right after the first training step, but rollout alone (`--debug-rollout-only`) is fine. Which knob does the usage guide point to first?
options: Increase `--rollout-num-gpus-per-engine`
Lower `--sglang-mem-fraction-static` so SGLang leaves room for Megatron's residual memory
Disable `--offload-train`
Switch `--ckpt-format` to torch
explain: Offloading is never perfect: Megatron keeps a few GB resident. The guide says that in colocated mode you must reduce SGLang's static memory fraction so both can coexist. Disabling train offload would make it worse.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
question: A rule fires because a user typed the wrong password three times. Using the NIST definitions, what is it so far?
options: An event that may be an adverse event; triage decides whether anything jeopardised systems or data
An incident, because a security rule fired
A false positive, because wrong passwords are normal
Nothing worth recording
explain: Failed logins are events. Whether they are adverse, and whether they add up to an incident (a password-guessing attack that succeeded, say), is exactly what triage decides. Calling it an incident or a false positive before looking skips the work.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Suspicious logins: impossible travel and MFA push spam
question: Impossible travel fires: a sign-in from Paris, then from Toronto 40 minutes later. Both passed MFA by the same phone, the Toronto IP belongs to the company's VPN provider, and the user agent and device ID match the user's laptop. Best verdict?
options: True positive: credentials stolen
False positive: the haversine formula is wrong
Undetermined: escalate to incident response
Benign true positive: the travel is impossible for a person but explained by the VPN; record it and suggest adding the VPN egress to the rule's known locations
explain: The rule correctly measured an impossible speed between two IPs, so it is not a false positive. The context (company VPN, same device, MFA passed on the user's phone) explains it, so it is benign. The note should feed a context fix, not a rule deletion.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
question: Mandiant's Snowflake investigation found that most stolen credentials had been exposed by infostealers long before use, some since 2020. Which control would have made those old credentials useless regardless of when they leaked?
options: Longer log retention
Requiring MFA (and network allow lists) on the accounts
A larger SOC team
Geolocation-based alerting
explain: Mandiant names missing MFA, unrotated credentials and missing network allow lists as the three factors. MFA and allow lists block a leaked password outright; logging and staffing only help you notice afterwards.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Talking to users, owners and leaders during an investigation
question: Which first line suits an update to leadership at hour two of an incident?
options: "We have run 140 queries across 6 data sources."
"Attack by a sophisticated nation-state."
"One laptop and one account compromised; contained; no evidence yet of data loss; next update 14:00 UTC."
"Too early to say anything."
explain: Bottom line first: impact, containment status, what is still unknown, when they will hear next. Activity counts tell leaders nothing, unsupported attribution misleads, and silence breeds rumours.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Why Johnny can't encrypt: usability is a security property
question: Which of Whitten and Tygar's properties explains why one accidental plaintext email is so serious?
options: The abstraction property
The barn door property
The unmotivated user property
The lack of feedback property
explain: Once the secret has been sent unprotected, nobody can be sure it was not read. Prevention has to happen before the mistake, because no fix after it restores secrecy.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing
question: A manager receives a voice message that sounds exactly like the CEO asking for an urgent transfer, followed by a text from a new number. Which response matches the IC3's guidance?
options: Reply to the text asking a personal question only the CEO would know
Listen for audio glitches; if none, proceed
Forward the voice message to a deepfake detection website and proceed if it says genuine
Call the CEO on a number already on record and confirm before doing anything
explain: The IC3 advises independently finding the person's number and calling to verify, and verifying new contact details through a previously confirmed channel. Personal questions can be researched, and detection is unreliable.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules
question: A building has three nested areas, and every door, including the server room, accepts a badge tap alone. Against NIST SP 800-116's table, what is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as the badges are encrypted
The limited and exclusion areas get only one factor instead of the two and three they need
There are too many doors
Badges should only be used at the front door
explain: Repeating the same factor at every door proves nothing new. The limited area needs two factors and the exclusion area three, for example badge plus PIN plus fingerprint.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
question: Before a physical test of a regional office, which ROE check would most directly have prevented the Iowa arrests?
options: Confirm that the client controls the building and that any other authority with jurisdiction has agreed or been informed
Use quieter tools
Test only during business hours
Wear company uniforms
explain: The conflict was over who controlled the courthouse and who had been told. Hours and attire matter, but authorisation from every party with control is the foundation.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Reading a latent: activating examples, logit effects, autointerp
question: Which check would most directly test the name 'promotes the token Paris' for a residual-stream latent?
options: Count how often the latent fires
Clamp the latent higher on prompts where it is off and measure whether the probability of ' Paris' rises
Raise its autointerp detection score
Look at its top five activating examples again
explain: The name is a claim about what the latent writes. An intervention measures that causally; activation-based scores and density only describe where it fires. The logit effect suggests it, and the clamp confirms it through the real network.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
question: A colleague says nearest neighbor is safest because it never invents values that were not measured. What is the main weakness of the resulting map?
options: It cannot be computed without a fitted variogram
It is discontinuous: the value jumps at Voronoi cell borders even when the true field is smooth
It always returns the global mean far from sensors
It gives every sensor the same weight
explain: Nearest neighbor copies the closest reading, so the map is a set of flat Voronoi tiles with steps at the borders. It needs no model, and far from sensors it still copies the nearest one rather than the mean.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
question: You have 5,000 weather stations and need a 1 km map nightly. Global ordinary kriging is too slow. Which change keeps most of kriging's benefits?
options: Switch to nearest neighbor
Krige from a local neighborhood of the nearest few dozen stations per target, using a variogram fitted once on all stations
Drop the variogram and set all weights to 1/5000
Use IDW with p = 0
explain: Local neighborhoods (like scikit-gstat's max_points or RBFInterpolator's neighbors) make each solve small. Distant stations get negligible weight beyond the range anyway, so the map changes little while cost drops sharply.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: Whisper's timestamp tokens are quantized to the native resolution. A word starts at 1.234 s. What is the closest timestamp the model can emit?
explain: Each encoder position covers 20 ms (30 s / 1500), and timestamp tokens are on the same 20 ms grid: ..., 1.22, 1.24, ... The nearest grid point to 1.234 s is 1.24 s. Finer word timings need extra machinery, such as the cross-attention alignment the openai/whisper code offers for word timestamps.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
question: A machine has 16 GiB of RAM, no swap and `vm.overcommit_memory = 0`. Processes A and B each malloc 12 GiB and each writes only its first 1 GiB. What most likely happens?
options: B's malloc returns NULL because 24 GiB exceeds RAM
Both mallocs succeed and both run normally: only touched pages use RAM
Both succeed, then the OOM killer immediately kills one of them
The kernel zeroes 24 GiB at malloc time and the machine swaps
explain: The default heuristic only rejects a single request bigger than RAM plus swap; 12 GiB is not, and it does not add up other processes' reservations. Frames are allocated on first touch, so about 2 GiB of RAM is used. Only if A and B actually wrote more than RAM holds would the OOM killer step in.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Where to add it, at which tokens, and how hard
question: A vector extracted at layer 6 of a 48-layer model works well at c = 4. A colleague adds the same vector at layer 40 with c = 4 and sees almost no effect. What is the most likely explanation?
options: At layer 40 the residual stream is much larger, so the same c is a much smaller relative push, and the concept may be represented differently there
Steering vectors only work in the first half of a network
Adding at a later layer reverses the sign of the vector
The model detects the vector and removes it
explain: Residual norms grow with depth, so a fixed-size vector becomes relatively small; on top of that, a direction found at layer 6 need not be the direction the concept uses at layer 40. Extract and inject at the same layer, and sweep c relative to the local norm.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
question: A team's refusal vector lowers the average refusal rate on held-out prompts from 60% to 20%. Which extra measurement best tests whether it is reliable?
options: The per-prompt slope of the behavior against the coefficient, and the fraction of prompts with a negative slope
A larger coefficient, to see whether the rate reaches 0%
The same average measured on the prompts used to build the vector
The norm of the vector compared with the residual stream
explain: Tan et al. show averages can hide many inputs that move the wrong way. Per-input slopes reveal that distribution directly. A larger coefficient changes the effect size, not its reliability; building-set scores leak; the norm ratio sets a scale but says nothing about consistency.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Windows, watermarks and allowed lateness, step by step
question: Rerun the toy with B = 7 s instead of 2 s (L still 5 s). Which readings are late or dropped?
options: e6 and e10 late, e12 dropped, exactly as before
No reading is late, and e12 is still dropped
Nothing is late or dropped
Every out-of-order reading is dropped
explain: When e6 arrives, max = 13 so W = 6 < 10: on time. When e10 arrives, max = 22 so W = 15 < 20: on time. e12 arrives with W = 27 - 7 = 20, past 10 + 5 = 15: still dropped. The price: window [0,10) now first fires at processing time 22.5 s (when e9 arrives) instead of 13.4 s.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
question: Why did the Transformer use scaled dot-product scores instead of Bahdanau's additive scores?
options: Both cost about the same in theory, but the dot product runs as one fast matrix multiplication; scaling fixes its weakness at large d_k
Additive scores cannot be trained with gradient descent
Dot products need no learned parameters at all, so the model is smaller
Additive scores only work with RNN hidden states
explain: Section 3.2.1 says the two have similar theoretical complexity and that dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice.
